I rise, not so much for the purpose of discussing this item, as to direct the attention of the House and especially the attention of the Government to the need of some immediate provision for the preservation of the public records of this country. I shall not attempt any elaborate review* of the necessity, but with due regard to the stage of the session, I shall endeavour to condense my remarks into the briefest possible compass. Therefore, I need not, in the first instance, emphasize the importance of preserving the records of public administration. That necessity has been realized in all civilized countries. I think it was Lord Salisbury who stated many years ago that "a nation which cannot produce its archives is like a bank that cannot redeem its paper currency with gold." Lord Durham also s*id: "A country without a history is not a nation," and a country cannot have a history in the true sense unless its records are preserved.
Let me state very briefly what has been done in Great Britain. In the year 1800 a committee of the House of Commons was appointed to make a report on the condition of public records in England and Scotland. As a result of this report, a Royal Commission was named, charged with the arrangement and publication of public records, and the control of all public repositories. This commission was renewed from year to year until 1837, and it issued many valuable publications. Up to that time no effective steps had been taken in Great Britain to ensure the safety of the records. With few exceptions, documents of the courts of law and government offices were stored at several places, mostly of an unsuitable nature, and the contents were inaccessible and unknown.
In 1837 an Act was passed. I have under my hand some details of its provisions, but it is not necessary that I should allude to them specially. It provided for the safety of the records, for their custody, for their classification and for the publication of information with regard to them. From the passing of this Act up to the present time, papers not required for the current business of administration in Great Britain have beeen removed to the Public Record Office, where they are arranged, classified and dealt with acording to regulations.
What has been done in the United States? I invite the attention of hon. gentlemen to this in particular, because in some respects the United States have given more attention and accomplished more work with regard to the history of Canada than we have done up to the present. In the United States they make no division between the two countries for historical purposes, and they have accomplished a great deal. The State Archives building in Wisconsin alone cost ten times more than the Canadian Archives building, and practically every state has an important building set aside for the purpose. The state of Michigan was perhaps the last to provide for its needs. In that state there was an enormous collection of historical material in the hands of Mr. Burton, which was known as the Burton Library. At a cost of several million dollars, the state purchased these documents which related to Michigan and to a portion of territory which was formerly Canadian. The collection is now state property, although it is still known as. the Burton collection.
In addition to the aid rendered by the state, enormous sums of money have been expended by private individuals on the history of the United States. The Carnegie Institute at Washington has an historical section, with a director at a salary of $10,000 a year. His duty is to find out in every part of the world material which will fill the gaps in American history. It is not his duty either to acquire documents or to copy them, but simply to tell the student where they are. For this purpose men have been sent to examine the Archives in France, England, Germany, Spain, Italy, Russia, Mexico, Cuba, Canada and other places. Guides are published of this material, including a volume of considerable size on Canada.
The Carter Brown Library in Rhode Island was founded many years ago by Mr. Carter, who left some millions of dollars for the purpose of collecting books and pamphlets previous to the year 1800 relating to North America. With the

interest on this money, a most valuable collection of books dealing with Canada and Newfoundland has been acquired. I believe that in the case now pending before the Privy Council between Canada and Newfoundland with regard to Labrador, it has been found necessary to resort to material which can be found in this collection and cannot be found anywhere within the limits of Canada. It is in this place, and in this place alone, that some of the most valuable hooks relating to Canada are to be found. As a further illustration, of many which might be given, I may say that the University of California possesses about two-thirds of the historical material relating to the province of British Columbia.
For these reasons the American universities are in a position to offer, and do offer, a far better course in history than can be offered anywhere in Canada. This will, in the course of time, have a serious effect on Canadian development, and it is certainly worthy of the most earnest and careful consideration by those who are entrusted with the government of this country.
What has Canada done? As far back as 1831 the Hon. Mr. Stuart introduced a resolution into the Assembly for a grant of money for the advancement of the knowledge of the history of the country. He thought it was most desirable that we should obtain a knowledge of how the French and English Governors had conducted the government of this country and of the progress that had been made. An interesting debate, to which I need not further allude, took place, but fifty years passed before the Government of Canada, in not a very effective way, undertook to make some provision for the preservation and classification of our Archives. Within the past fifteen or eighteen years there have been more liberal appropriations for the purpose, and I am glad to recall the fact that under the administration of Sir Wilfrid Laurier a building for the housing of the Archives was provided. That building, as I shall attempt to point out, has become absolutely and absurdly inadequate for the purpose for which it was intended.
Through indifference and failure in the past to provide a safe place for the Archives of this country, many of the most important documents have been destroyed, and but for the foresight of the English and French Governors in insisting on duplicates and triplicates of official documents, Canada would not be in a position to-day to understand much of her past history or to obtain the documents to con-

duct her negotiations relating to treaties, boundaries, fisheries and lands. Without the materials for history it is perfectly obvious to hon. gentlemen that we can only have meagre text books in our schools, and that the teaching of history in our universities must be poor. In that case our people will grow up with but a limited knowledge of our progress and of its tendencies and characteristics, and we shall be less fitted than we otherwise would be to cope with present and future problems.
I should like to direct the attention of hon. members, and particularly the atten tion of the Prime Minister and his col leagues, to the report which was made b5 the Royal Commission appointed by the Canadian Government in 1912. I refer to it in the first place to show the extreme insecurity in which very valuable records are placed at the present time. I quote from the report of that commission, which was composed of Sir Joseph Pope, Undersecretary of State for External Affairs, Mr. E. F. Jarvis, Assistant Deputy Minister of Militia and Defence, and Dr. Arthur G. Doughty, Dominion Archivist. First, as to the state of preservation of public documents, I quote as follows:
This varies. In most of the departments, while the current correspondence is well kept, the older documents are commonly relegated to basements, attics and dark rooms, apparently rather as lumber to be got rid of than as records to be preserved, and too frequently are not so arranged as to admit of ready reference, or in not a few instances, even of convenient access. In some cases there is no semblance of method, the older papers being stored in inaccessible places, without pretence of classification, or any precise indication as to what the collection may contain. The exposure of the documents to dust, dampness, and other agencies, and in some cases their proximity to the heating apparatus of the building, contribute t,o the deterioration of the papers, while the inflammable nature of the shelving on which they are placed is a constant source of danger.
The report goes on to say, that in most eases these documents are not required for use in the office beyond a period of five years back, and it is said that "the experience of the Militia Department (the only department which so far has transferred its old records to the Archives), is that these inquiries can he answered more satisfactorily by the Archivist, to whom all such questions are referred."
Now comes a very important part of the report, as to the character of the buildings in which records of priceless value for historical purposes are kept at present:
As regards this feature there is no uniformity. In some departments the files of correspondence,

of whatever age, are contained in steel cabinets and are readily accessible. In others, many of the older documents are stored away in wooden cupboards or boxes, sometimes loosely piled on shelves, or, it may be, on the floor of basement or attic rooms, where they lie for years, dustladen and forgotten, offering scant facilities for examination, and in some instances well-nigh inaccessible. The rooms in the upper stories of most buildings in which these documents are lodged are totally unfit for the storage of valuable records. The wood is old and dry and there would be little prospect of saving any of the papers in the event of fire. One fact, everywhere observable, is that the preservation and care of the older records is the last thought of anybody.	_	.	,
The congested condition of the offices owing to the lack of room is no doubt largely responsible for this state of affairs, as in many departments the ingenuity of the higher officials is sorely taxed to find space in which to transact current business. Under these conditions it is not surprising that documents rarely, if ever, required for the conduct of the day's work, should be relegated to dark rooms and passages not suitable for other uses.
Then the report goes on to point out that thousands of documents are stored in buildings throughout the city in upper rooms, with old fashioned wooden staircases. These papers are in various stages of neglect, with no protection of any sort against fire. To indicate the volume of these records, I may point out, as stated in the report of the commission, the following facts: In the East Block alone there are 69 rooms with 308,810 cubic feet, 7,178 drawers, 22,633 lineal feet of shelves devoted to the storage of records. In the West Block there are 74 rooms, 353,473 cubic feet, 13,662 drawers, 7,538 lineal feet of shelves. In the old Parliament building there were 22 rooms, 66,594 cubic feet, 2,082 drawers, 10,240 lineal feet of shelves. In the Langevin block and other buildings there are 283 rooms, 901,137 cubic feet, 69,950 drawers, and 86,808 lineal feet of shelves. These figures give a grand total of 438 rooms, 1,629,014 cubic feet, 92,872 drawers, and 127,219 lineal feet of shelves. In other words, there are over 24 miles of shelves. The report indicates that a very large quantity of these documents might be destroyed under competent authority, and it is urged that they should be classified at once and that those of value should be removed immediately to a special fire-proof building provided for the purpose.
This report was made immediately before the war, and during the stress and anxiety of conditions due thereto, it was not acted upon, although, perhaps, it should have been, even under those conditions. As a matter of fact, an Order in Council was passed a few months before war began
to give effect to the recommendations of the commission, and a sum of money was placed in the Estimates for the construction of the necessary building, but owing to the war the proposal was not carried out.
I am reminded by my hon. friend the member for East Hamilton (Mr. Mewburn), that among those documents to which I have alluded are records of absolutely priceless value relating to the achievements and,records of the Canadian Expeditionary Force. I am told that there are about 700,000 such files in the Rea building, which is not fireproof, and that material, the destruction of which would shock the country, may at any time be destroyed unless some adequate measures are taken for its preservation. In addition, I should like to emphasize the point, which I made a moment ago, that even for the material under the care of the Dominion Archivist, the space at his command is absolutely and utterly insufficient.
I should be very glad indeed if any word of mine could bring to the attention of hon. members of this House the very great importance of the work which has been accomplished in the Archives during the past fifteen or twenty years, in securing, preserving and classifying the records of Canada. I recollect very well when Dr. Doughty was brought to Ottawa to take charge of the Archives of this country.
I recall the discussions which we had in the House, and I look back with some satisfaction to the fact that I did everything possible to encourage him to continue in the work which he had undertaken. He was a little discouraged at first on account of the inadequacy of the financial provision for his work, and I remember that from the side of the House which I then occupied, we did venture to urge upon the Government, and especially upon the then Minister of Agriculture, a somewhat larger appropriation. Dr. Doughty is a man whose service is of very great value to this country in the work which he is carrying on. In the first place, he has all the zeal and zest of an enthusiast. His whole heart is in his work, and he has, besides, the system and the organizing capacity of a business man. These two qualifications are but seldom united in one person and they have enabled him to be of the greatest possible service to this country.
In that connection, let me add a word in regard to the work which is being carried on by the Board of Historical Publications. That board consists of Dr. Adam

Shortt, as chairman; Dr. Doughty, the Dominion archivist; Prof. George M. Wrong, of Toronto University; Prof. Charles W. Colby, of McGill University, and the Hon. Thomas Chapais, a member of the Senate. The object of the board is to put at the immediate and convenient service of all persons in any way interested in Canadian history the most essential documents bearing on the development of the vital interests of the Canadian people. A vast amount of documental and other material relating to the early history of this country has been gathered together, and perhaps I could sum up the work of the board in a word. In a certain sense, and to a certain extent, the Board of Historical Publications acts as the interpreter, to the people of Canada and to the rest of the world, of the material which has been and is being gathered together in the Archives. Much of this material has been brought to light only recently, through the activities of the Archives Department. The very volume of it and the labour entailed in making thorough researches has hitherto deterred all but a few enthusiasts from making full use of it. The work of the board has been to organize such research and to put out such publications as will make the labours of the Dominion Archivist and his staff available generally to Canadian people, and particularly to those interested in historical research. It is claimed, and_ I think with justice, that the effect of this is greatly to broaden the basis of Canadian history, to impart a new interest in that history to those who at present are practically indifferent, and also to make for a more intelligent, practical, and wholesome national sentiment. I hope the committee will bear with me if I read just a word from an address upon the work of the Board of Historical Publications, which was delivered by Dr. Adam Shortt, chairman, before the Royal Society of Canada in 1919. He said:
Owing- to the peculiar relations which Canada [DOT]bore to the Mother Country, both as a French and as an English colony, and the necessity for a constant interchange of information and instructions, special facts, views, and interests there was. produced and accumulated a remarkable body of documentary records embodying the chief facts of Canadian history. There is a greater variety than might be expected, in the presentation of the facts and views, since there were several effective channels, public and private, through which these might 'be presented and appeals made to the imperial authorities. Thus in the long run most currents of colonial life were represented in one form or another, whether for approval or condemnation, in criticism or defence. Much local material, considerable private correspondence, 
and many descriptive accounts of the country and the condition of the people have been preserved and recovered. Early newspapers and pamphlets, though many of them rare or unique, and quite scattered in their location, are also extant and furnish a very necessary atmosphere of fact and comment for the more central and official documents. Owing to the very volume of this material, even so far as collected at the Archives in Ottawa, and more so as scattered in various Canadian centres, it is possible for only a very limited number of students to consult it. To do so requires at once a strong personal interest, a special historical training, the necessary leisure, and last, but far from least, the requisite means, to enable one at all adequately to consult the documentary and other evidence necessary to satisfactory results.
Further on he says:
If, therefore, our Canadian history is to be known in authentic form, not only to our own people, but to the outside world, whose interest in Canada is steadily rising, it requires the facilities for direct knowledge to be greatly increased. It is necessary to put in available form the chief documents relating to the various phases of the country's history.
I have only quoted very slightly from this pamphlet. I understand that a number of copies are available for the information of hon. gentlemen and any of them would find the pamphlet well worth a perusal. It gives a comprehensive outline of the programme which the board has undertaken.
I should have alluded, in speaking of the nation's loss, to the very great loss we sustained when the old Parliament Buildings were destroyed a few years ago. At that time a mass of material went up in flames, the loss of which is absolutely irreparable seeing that this material bore directly, in many ways, upon the history of this country. In examining the currents of thought bearing upon the legislation presented to Parliament, we have a most valuable guide to the tendency of public opinion from time to time, and to the progress and development- of the national thought. All that material and much other information, the nature of which will readily occur to hon. gentlemen, has absolutely been lost; and fifty times as much is to-day in danger of being lost through the accidental occurrence of a fire against which no precautions are being taken at present.
I spoke of the valuable services of Dr Doughty. Let me also observe that in my opinion Dr. Shortt has a knowledge, an ability and an experience which have enabled him to be of the greatest service to this country. His work in the past has largely been in the historical line. His whole heart is in his work, and he is very ably assisted by Dr. Doughty, and by the three gentlemen whom I have mentioned whose labours are entirely unremunerated

by the country because they are labours of love, and whose work with Dr. Shortt and Dr. Doughty has gone on most harmoniously and effectively.
Now, I realize that we are under conditions when any proposal for increased expenditure must be examined very carefully by hon. gentlemen, and by the Government who must initiate it, before any such proposal will find favour. But we do make appropriations in respect of the material affairs of this country. No one,
I am sure, will minimize the importance of our material progress and development.
I can look back for more than half a century in realizing the remarkable advance in standards of living among the people since my boyhood days. And we need not fear as to our future development. But crops and manufactures do not make up the whole life of a nation. The development of the intellectual and spiritual qualities of the nation, of the moral qualities of the people, is surely not of less importance. A nation which neglects these higher considerations cannot hold its place in the world. The preservation of our records has a direct relation to such considerations. I do strongly urge that some appropriation for the purpose should be made before the conclusion of 4 p.m. the present session.
I offer this last observation. Looking back over the history of the world we may learn that what men have presently regarded as immaterial and unsubstantial has proved in the lapse of centuries most material in that it is most enduring. The Forum and the Coliseum are in ruins, but the history, the literature and the jurisprudence of Rome will always survive.

I think the
House will agree with the right hon. member for Kings (Sir Robert Borden) that it is most important that there should be suitable and adequate accommodation for the public records of this country. I think we all recognize that the circumstance of the war coming at the time it did, and occasioning efforts in so many directions, has really been responsible for an accumulation of material of priceless value the coming into existence of which could not be foreseen at the time the original Archives building was erected. Any hon. member who has visited the Archives will have seen how overcrowded the buildings have been for many years. The need, I think, is obvious and the purpose is as worthy a one as the House could be called upon to support.

I only regret that the
right hon. gentleman when he was Prime Minister, and when there was still some money in the Treasury, should not have carried out the conclusions of the report which he read a moment ago. I am, however, in entire accord with the remarks made by him. I think, as Lord Salisbury said, a country which has no Archives is like a bank which cannot redeem its currency in gold; and by the way, my right hon. friend quoted from Lord Durham a remark which is, in a sense, historic. It is true that Lord Durham said a country without a history is not a nation. He said that on the occasion of his famous report, and it was directed against the minority in this country-at that time the majority. But the answer came afterwards, and showed that there was a wealth of records and Archives in the country, thus establishing the right of the French Canadians to consider themselves as a nation with a history. Because, as my right hon. friend knows, that remark was at once taken up by the most remarkable historian that Canada has produced so far-I refer to F. X. Garneau-who wrote a work which is considered a standard book; and if you read the introduction written by his grandson, in the fourth edition of Garneau's "History of Canada," you will find that it was that very remark of Durham which prompted Garneau to write the history of his country. And his book, as I stated a moment ago, is considered, not only in America but in Europe, as a standard book.
Mr. Chairman, the right hon. gentleman is quite correct when he says that we should be more careful about our national records, whcih are to be found not only in Canada but even in the United States. I remember reading some years ago a series of books written by the late Mr. Roosevelt dealing with the history of the far West, and in a footnote he stated that he had based his work on documents obtained in what was originally part of New France, that is, in some of the Western States. The Champlain Society is an American society, but mostly all its published documents are of Canadian origin. This society has published the Relations des Jesuites, which is a most important series of documents of old French Canada. My right hon. friend spoke of the work accomplished under the inspiration of the late Mr. Stuart, a member of the old Assembly in 1831. As we all know, the documents which were collected under the Union were all lost in the fire which destroyed the Parliament build-

ings in Montreal in 1849. I heard the late Mr. P. J. 0. Chauveau state on more than one occasion-and he was himself a member of that Assembly-that invaluable records were destroyed on that occasion. But since that date Canada has been able to collect a large number of very important documents, both originals and duplicates, relating to her history. We owe a debt of gratitude especially to the late Mr. Brymner, and also to his successor, Dr. Doughty; but we must not forget that it was our late beloved Sfriend, the Hon. Sydney Fisher, who undertook to give our Archives a repository in this city. It was when he was acting Minister of Public Works that he induced Parliament to vote a sum of money to erect our Archives building. I quite admit that it is now inadequate, but there is space on both sides, and for a reasonable sum of money the present building could be extended to provide the accommodation which is now so urgently needed. I must not forget, too, that nearly all our Governors General have helped us in enriching our Archives, and especially the late Earl Grey. It was under Earl Grey that the Government of Canada became the possessor of all the official despatches exchanged between the Canadian and Home Governments since British domination. Those despatches, commissions, etc., were in London, but thanks to the intervention of Lord Grey they have now come into our possession. If it is decided to enlarge the Archives building, I would suggest that as the Royal Society is officially recognized and subsidized to a certain extent by the Government, the buildings be so\ arranged that the annual meetings of the society may be held there and their library and records be deposited there. Several resolutions to that effect have been passed by the Royal Society, and it seems to me that they should be carried out.
While I quite agree with the right hon. gentleman that the present Archives building is absolutely inadequate and is insufficiently protected against fire, I must at the same time express my profound regret at the wanton destruction of the many invaluable documents which took place a few months ago in this city. On several occasions I have asked the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Meighen) to lay on the table of the House what is known as the Snider report. I shall not discuss it now as it is not before the House, but it is unfortunately only too true that thousands and thousands-I do

not exaggerate-of records and blue books were destroyed, whether from ignorance or wilfully I cannot say. I cannot believe that it was due to the mere lust of destruction; but if it was through ignorance, that ignorance was almost criminal. I do not wish to accuse any one, although rumours are very thick on the subject in the city; but if it is found that officials having some grey matter in their heads took upon themselves to destroy those thousands of documents, many of which cannot be duplicated to-day, certainly criminal proceedings should be taken against them. I have been told that there were books, reports and records in that mass of destroyed documents which could not be replaced. For instance, there were maps dating from the time of the first French settlement in Canada, there were reports dating from the beginning of the British domination, and there were many blue books and reports dating before Confederation. Yet some officials of the Government, I am told, had the audacity to order the destruction of those documents. Once more I must protest against this wanton destruction, and I hope that when the right hon. gentleman receives Mr. Justice Snider's report he will take the necessary steps to prosecute the authors of that destruction.

Mr. Chairman, I happen to know a little about this affair. As chairman of the Committee on Printing, I took occasion to make a short investigation as to how much damage was ,done. As a matter of fact I found that no documents of any value to the country were destroyed.
How do you know?
We have a list of all the documents that were there.
I am told it is incomplete.

The hon. gentleman is all wrong. In fact, the documents stowed away were duplicates, and the Committee on Printing decided that they should be distributed to the various public libraries throughout the country, and that was in process of being done when somebody in the department or some of these outside people who were cleaning up the department, when they came upon statutes of say 1918, 1917, 1916 and earlier, which were all duplicates, fired them out of the place to make room for other documents. Some of the older duplicates had

been lying there for years and nobody took any notice of them. This is just a tempest in a teapot. None of the big libraries will lose these duplicates, because we can easily replace them; duplicate volumes can be obtained from the departments and other places. As to the matter of burning or destroying them, thousands of books of this description are destroyed every year in the departments. They take up room and lumber the scenery; some one comes along and says: "Who wants all this stuff here?" or perhaps a "new broom" comes in and sweeps clean, as in this case. A change was being made in the department; a branch was being transferred down to the Printing Bureau, and there was a great accumulation of stuff there. Well, after this had been done, several officials in the department who are always making themselves a little busy and trying to exaggerate their own importance, raised a big row about it. The question has been raised as to who was the author of that order. Now, Judge Snider heard evidence here, and from my information in the matter Judge Snider did not act just as fairly as he should-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think the entire
discussion with reference to the judge is out of order. It is entirely wrong to refer to a judge in that way.

I do not want the hon. member for Maisonneuve to give the impression that thousands of documents and old maps of value were destroyed. There is not an old map of Canada of any value which cannot be found in the Archives. There was no document of any value in that room which cannot be found in the Parliamentary Library and in the various departments. There were duplicate volumes of publications of the departments which the departments did not wish to retain, and these accumulated as they always have accumulated. They were not valuable at all. I have seen the list of documents which was prepared with a view to seeing how many could be dispensed with. The intention was to do away with some anyway and to select a certain number of volumes to be sent to the various libraries, but unfortunately before the selection was made some one gave an order for their destruction. But there is no great loss to the country, as the hon. gentleman would have seen if he had taken the trouble to make an investigation into the matter. Unfortunately we cannot now go into the
question of Judge Snider's report, but when that report comes in I will take occasion to discuss it.

The matter which my right hon. friend from King's (Sir Robert Borden) has brought before the committee this afternoon is one of no small importance. In the various matters which come before this House we are prone to give the main consideration to those things that are more or less material in character.
I quite agree with the sentiment expressed by my right hon. friend that those things which have to do with the history of a country, with the character and intimate life of its people and of those who have preceded the present generation, should be of very considerable interest to those who are legislating now. The present condition so far as our public records and documents are concerned cannot be satisfactory to any one who has regard for his country's interests. We have a building which is altogether inadequate for the housing of these records. My right hon. friend has given the details of the manner in which a great many of our public records are now stored. Take the East block and the West block; if a fire should take place in either of those buildings their interior construction is such that everything within them would be destroyed. There is wood there which has been drying almost for generations; everything is of a highly inflammable character and the loss that the country might sustain would be very great indeed. I have often thought, Mr. Chairman as I have wandered into the Library adjacent to this building, how easily a fire could sweep everything within its walls and destroy all the books, many of which are of rare value. I think this is a matter which should at the proper time, and as early as possible, receive the consideration of the Government and of Parliament.
Allusion has been made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) to the value of the documents that were recently destroyed. I am not going to interpose in the difference of opinion between my hon. friend from North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) and my hon. friend from Maisonneuve as to the value of these documents; from what I have heard they were of very considerable value. But does this not emphasize the pressing need of some better system of handling the public records than we have, so that these records may from time to time be scrutinized by those who are competent to do so

with a view to determining their historical value and placing those which are of value beyond the possibility of loss? We are voting this year $20,000,000 for militia, naval, police and air services. I suggest that Parliament might very well take one million dollars of that vote and devote it to the purpose of providing proper housing for our public records. This is a matter which should be taken up without delay; the public documents should be carefully surveyed and those of historical value set aside for future generations. The members of the committee are indebted to my right hon. friend from King's for bringing this matter to their attention.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I would not for a moment question the wisdom of a policy of reasonable generosity in public expenditure for the purpose of preserving to the country the records, dispatches, communications, and other documents that we already have, and those that accrue from year to year. The importance of such preservation multiplies as years advance, and it always looks the smallest just at the time when the necessity for the outlay of money is before us. I do not think that Canada can be said to have been negligent in the matter of collecting, systematizing -and, indeed, up to now, preserving, or at least arranging for their preservation- the historical records of the country, nor do I think there is any neglect at the present time in that regard. Great care has been taken, so far back as I have had any occasion to traverse, to see that, nothing was lost, so far as loss could be avoided. Pains have been taken, indeed, to collect everything that could assist enlightened discussion in future, and that would be necessary for accurate historical survey. In making the collection, possibly, we have not provided the outlay necessary for its safe preservation. We have been very unfortunate in that regard. I do not know that it can be attributed to neglect; it is attributable much more to accident. The loss of the Legislative Buildings at Montreal in 1849, and of the Parliament Buildings in this city in 1916 were very great disasters. Perhaps the most deplorable feature of the disasters was the destruction of just such material as we ought to cherish, such as is under discussion now. There can be no question that, at the moment, we are very much in arrear in providing suitable building accommodation for the Archives, and we are all along running very substantial risks in keeping such archives as we now possess in the various buildings through-
out the city in which they are stored. Those buildings are not in keeping with the valuable nature of the documents lodged there, which we ought carefully to preserve. We must, remember, however, that for outlay upon public buildings in this city, a tremendous demand fell upon us when the Parliament buildings were destroyed in 1916. Under the stress of ' the war, under the load of obligations which the war brought upon us, we had to address ourselves to the task of renewing on this Hill this commodious and magnificent pile, an effort that in itself has entailed an expenditure running already into many millions, though the work is not yet complete; an expenditure which, I venture now to express the opinion, has been well made; an expenditure which would have to be vastly increased if the structure had to be replaced now. On the whole, while, perhaps, errors may have been made, the conduct of the entire construction has been creditable to the country.
What I set out to say in that regard, however, was merely this: that the work has imposed upon the public treasury a burden of an unprecedented character for public buildings in Ottawa. We had to provide the Hunter building in the city because of the expansion of the public service during the war, and the certainty that that building, at least, would be necessary afterwards. Indeed, there are many more ' buildings which we shall have to continue to lease for many years. In a word, we have had to confine ourselves to essentials, and when I use the word "esesntials," I use it in, perhaps, its narrowest sense; because it might well include just such accommodation as had been so eloquently urged by the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) this afternoon. All I am in a position to state at the moment with regard to that, is that the matter will be taken into consideration as soon as we feel that we can at all justify an expenditure of this nature.
Some reference has been made to a particular destruction of documents that occurred in this city, I think, about a year ago, and in relation to which an investigation under the Inquiries Act has been under way for some time by Judge Snider, of the County Court of Wentworth. It is not altogether appropriate, in fact, I doubt if it is in order, that there should be any discussion as to the circumstances connected with that loss, whatever the loss may be, pending the report and its pre-

sentation to this House. I observe a wide difference of opinion between the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) and the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Currie) as to the loss that has occurred. I will not venture to decide between them, or to express an opinion at all. I shall be surprised if the loss goes quite the length feared by the hon. member for Maisonneuve, and I shall be delighted if it is no greater than that stated by the hon. member for Simcoe North. Suffice it to say this, that when the report is received the House will be in a position to judge from both the evidence and the finding, how much of that destruction, whatever its extent may be, is attributable to accident, how much to ignorance, how much to stupidity, how much to malignity, and how much to crime, if any. When we have the report before us, then will be^ the time to discuss the matter; and I think we might well abide that event before making up our minds to see that somebody goes to gaol because, unfortunately, documents have been lost.
All I will say in conclusion, is that I appreciate the manner in which the right hon. gentleman has pressed his views upon the House, and I hope that the evidence of their acceptability, that now is apparent everywhere around me, will be present when any appropriation that the Government desires to submit to the House is before the committee for review.

I am very
glad that the Prime Minister and his colleagues will take this matter into consideration, and I hope their consideration will result in some action, which I think is sorely needed. May I be permitted to associate myself with what the hon. member for Maisonneuve has said with regard to the service of Dr. Brymner and also with regard to the assistance afforded to this country by Lord Grey while he was Governor General. I should like to add that Lord Minto was also most zealous and active in the assistance which he gave to the Dominion Archivist and the people of this country generally in securing documents of great value from other countries.

In reference to the
destruction of these documents, they were not original documents, I understand; they were simply surplus copies of blue books and statutes. A department publishes a blue book and issues it throughout the country. A certain number of volumes that
the people do not take, are sent always to the junk pile.

How does the hon. member
know?

As I stated before, 1
saw a list of them, and I think I have a list upstairs in my room.

It is admitted by archivists of eminence in the country that the documents were most invaluable. Some of them cannot be found in the Library to-day.
Item stands.
Railways and Canals,-chargeable to Income -Trent canal improvements, $515,000.

When this item was
under discussion a few days ago, I gave the details of the expenditure. Does the committee want the details again.

I should like to have some
information as to the details of this item.

This sum is to be
expended on the following work: New lock and dam at Bobcaygeon, $205,000; at Lake-field, $40,000; Otonabee river dams, Nassau, $175,000; construction of lock gauge, $25,000; reservoir dams, $25,500; Mississauga lake dams, $8,000; concrete railings for river walls, $6,000; painting lift locks, $6,000; miscellaneous works, $9,500; total, $515,000.

Would it not have
been better to include the details in the Estimates?
It has always been the custom to give the total amount in the Estimates, and to give the committee the details.

What amount of
tonnage passed through this canal on which we are spending so much money, last year, for instance?
The total tonnage that passed through the whole length is about 50,000, but, of course, the waterway is not open all the way through the Georgian bay, but only from Trenton to Orillia.

Is any record kept
of the number of ships that pass through the canal?

The officers along the
canal send the information in to the Statistics Branch, which is under the Department of Trade and Commerce.

If I might be allowed
to make reference to this matter in answer

to some of the inquiries that have been made by hon. members, I may say that for many years I have lived in the neighbourhood of this Trent Canal system. As to the history of this Nassau dam, on October 27, 1896, when the Hon. A. G. Blair was Minister of Railways and Canals, an agreement was entered into between the Dominion Government and the Bank of Commerce, which was the owner of the riparian rights in the property adjacent to the Nassau dam, by which the property was conveyed to the Dominion Government on certain terms. The question of power rights arose, the Bank of Commerce owning those rights, and the Government being desirous of constructing a section of the canal running from Nassau to east and south of the city of Peterborough. It became necessary for the Government to make terms with the Bank of Commerce, and those terms were briefly these: that the Government should receive a conveyance of these lands and of the rights attached to them at Nassau in return for the'maintenance of this dam. The dam was a wooden structure, and as time went on it became necessary to reconstruct it. There is so much leakage through it that the Canadian General Electric Company, which has acquired the dam from the Bank of Commerce, finds that the surplus water which . they are entitled to use for power purposes has been so seriously affected that they are now requiring the Government to carry out the terms of that agreement. The dam is in a state of disrepair so serious that it is affecting the power rights of the company, and the company unquestionably is taking a course which it has a right to take in insisting that the provisions of the agreement which was entered into' in 1896 be carried out.
There are some other items in the Estimates which I submit are very important, and for these reasons. In the city of Peterborough there are at present a number of flour mills with a large daily capacity. The Quaker Oats Company has a capacity of 8,000 barrels per day; Peterborough Cereal, 1,000 barrels per day; and the Campbell Flour Mills 750 barrels per day of food products, chiefly flour. We on the Trent waterway feel that it is very important that the canal be constructed through to Georgian bay so that the wheat may come down from Georgian bay at a cheaper rate to Peterborough, which is a milling centre, and to Campbellford. There are also a number of foundries located in Peterborough and Belleville. Midland is a town which for many years

has had for sale a large amount of pig iron, and that has been very expensive to obtain in these cities where the foundries are. So it is very important for the people of the cities of Peterborough and Belleville and the town of Campbellford, that a sum of money should be expended annually on this waterway in order that the construction may be completed, for it is only partially constructed at the present time.
The suggestion has been made that the tonnage carried is small. I would point out that there are numbers of fleets of gasoline launches plying along that waterway, and also steamboat lines, and I cannot for one moment believe that the tonnage carried by these gasoline boats is included in that 53,000 tons which has been given as the total tonnage carried through the canal, because these gasoline boats travel between various points along the waterway, for example, between Hastings and Peterborough, between Campbellford and east and south, and not through the whole canal, so I think the figure mentioned is not a fair estimate of the total tonnage carried along the waterway.
The waterway from Trenton to Georgian bay is about 200 miles long, owing to the connecting navigable rivers and extensive lakes in that country. On the other hand, there is a shore line of over 1,000 miles in this district along the waterway, and it serves a population larger than some of the provinces. Within ten miles of the shore line there are six million acres of forest, mineral and agricultural lands. Millions of feet of lumber are manufactured in the immediate district from the logs that come down through this waterway, and these dams are necessary in order to carry out the Government's agreement with the lumber companies to maintain water enough to float these logs in certain seasons of the year.
The Dominion Government entered into an agreement with the Ontario Government, which was confirmed by Order in Council on July 22, 1905, whereby the Dominion Government took over,, all the locks, dams, water rights, and the flooded lands in this whole watershed and area, and in return it was given by the Ontario Government all the property in these locks, swing bridges and other property which the Ontario Government owned and controlled. The Dominion Government was required to keep this reservoir area constructed, and is under covenant to do it to-day, for the purpose of keeping suffici-

ent water in the reservoirs for the purposes of the different lumber companies operating in the district. I submit, therefore, that it is very important that not only the Nassau dam construction should be carried on at the present time, but also that the rest of these works on which we have been spending money for some years should be carried on. The work has stood for a considerable length of time by reason of the war, which was a reason for delay in everything, but these works should now be gone on with in order to preserve the property.
There is one point to which I wish to direct the minister's attention, and that is the fair wage clause that is in the agreement between the contractor on the Nassau dam and the department. It is said that outside labour is being brought in from some of the large cities, 'and paid a very low wage, as low as 35 cents an hour, while the fair wage in Peterborough is 50 cents an hour. That is the rate which the city corporation and contractors generally are paying, yet the contractors on the dam, I understand, are bringing in men at 35 cents an hour. This is hardly fair to the unemployed in the city of Peterborough, of whom we have a number at the present time, and I think that there should be an investigation made by the minister to ascertain what wage is actually being paid by the contractor on the Nassau dam, and if he is not paying a fair wage, the matter should be reported to the Department of Labour, so that it can insist, under the fair wage clause, on a fair wage being paid to these men, the fair wage being the current wage in the city of Peterborough at the present time. I think also some attempt should be made to prevent bringing in from the large cities numbers of unemployed at 35 cents an hour, if that is taking place, and I am informed that it is. But I do urge upon hon. members, who are perhaps inclined to question the need of these expenditures at the present time, that there is a real necessity for them, because if this work is ever to be of any considerable value we must have a complete waterway from Georgian bay down to lake Ontario.

In these items there
is one large amount for Bobcaygeon lock. I have been there myself and I considered that the lock was in a very dangerous condition. I do not know whether hon. members know the situation, but we are proceeding with that work now for the
simple reason that the engineer is firmly of opinion that further delay would be disastrous. With regard to the question of wages, all contracts contain a fair wage clause, and if there is any trouble, complaint is usually made to the Minister of Labour, who investigates the matter and brings about an adjustment between the contractor and the employees.

I conferred with the
Minister of Labour to-day on this matter and he informed me that the usual practice was for the department in which any question of this kind arose to make the investigation, and if there were found to be any ground for complaint, then it was referred to him for determination. With reference to the Bobcaygeon lock, this structure for some years has been in a state of disrepair, and when I visited it last it was leaking and unquestionably required either to be renewed or to be reconstructed. I visited the locality a couple of months ago, and the engineers are extending the canal through the centre of the town along the old line of the canal, making it somewhat deeper, and broadening the lock to some extent. The town is partly torn up along the course of the canal, and it is absolutely necessary that the work should be completed, because at the present time the debris is all piled up about the streets and on the highways. I do not see what can be done but to go on and finish this work, which is one of the most essential public works that are required just now. The work at the Nassau dam also requires to be done, in view of the covenant of the Government with the Canadian General Electric.
I endorse the remarks of the member for Peterborough (Mr. Gordon) about completing this work, which has been under way for a great many years.

There is an item following this, dealing with completion work on the Trent canal. This item deals with improvements. If the hon. member intends to speak on the question of the completion of the canal he might wait for a few minutes.

The reason why I
suggested that these items which the minister mentions should be set out in the Estimates was that we might take them up one by one. It is quite possible that we might be satisfied to pass some of the items and not others. Personally, I am satis-

fied that some of the work which the minister recommends is in order, but I am not at all satisfied that some of the rest of it should be proceeded with. Some of it can readily stand. It is difficult to decide just what to do in a case of this kind. We do not want to hold out against the whole item, and there is no way of deciding just what should be passed. It is quite probable that the Bobcaygeon item should go through, but with reference to some of the others, which I heard mentioned in a casual way and which I do not quite recollect at the moment, I think they could easily stand over until another year. The minister, the other day, intimated that his department was trying to follow a scheme of economy in connection with certain works which he said could not be carried out this season. Well, I submit that this is a case in which there is room for the exercise of that economy. Item 115 is for construction in connection with the Trent canal and the Welland canal. This item deals with repairs. These other items are as follows:

one of these expenditures although we have tried to keep them down as well as possible.
Is it necessary to complete that work at Bobcaygeon this year?

It is under contract
and we must complete the work this year.

The engines and pumps, and everything in connection with the work, are still running and it is simply impossible to leave it as it is at the present time -it would cause the loss of many thousands of dollars.

If it is simply the loss of many thousands of dollars that is involved I can point out to the minister many other instances in other parts of Canada where similar losses are being occasioned from a failure to proceed with public works. When the Government took this canal over from the Ontario Government there were many old locks on the system in such a dilapidated condition that they must be renewed at some time or other. Is the new lock at

When the minister was

In the western provinces, where the natural resources are still retained by the Federal Government, the lumbermen have to construct their own dams and keep the waterways in shape for running their logs. In view of this fact, I would like to know why it is that the Government is doing such work here.

As I explained a few minutes ago, the Dominion Government in 1905, took over from the Ontario Government all the dams on the Trent waterway and agreed to maintain them so that the lumbermen could float their logs through. The Ontario Government had made that agreement with the lumbermen. If we do not now keep those dams in repair we are liable for any damages that the lumbermen may sustain.
Is it not necessary to keep those dams in repair for conservation purposes?
That was part of the scheme.
Does the agreement with the Ontario Government entail additional construction work by the Federal Government?	[DOT]
I have not the agreement here, but generally the Federal Government agreed to maintain the waterway so that it could be operated as it was prior to our taking it over.
But not to extend or enlarge it in any way?
I cannot say, I know we have to keep the system in order for operation.
My hon. friend (Mr. Sexsmith) suggested that it is necessary to keep this canal in repair for transportation.
For conservation purposes.

And other purposes. In regard to transportation, we are told that 53,000 tons of freight went

through this canal at an annual operating cost of $97,000 for wages alone. I would rather see an item in the Estimates for the transportation free of charge on our railways of the traffic that is now being carried on this canal rather than keep this white elephant any longer. It is not an undertaking for the benefit of Canada generally, it is purely local, in fact almost a municipal undertaking. It is unfortunate that the Dominion Government should have put its head in a noose and been cinched up in this way by the Provincial Government.

The Dominion Government, rightly or wrongly, agreed to maintain this waterway, and to protect the flow of the waters. There is no way of getting over that agreement without paying damages. But in my judgment when this waterway is completed to the Georgian bay
How many miles remain to be built?

From the Georgian
bay end to Washago is about thirty miles. When I come to the next item I have a memorandum of what it will cost to complete this waterway through to Georgian bay.

An hon. member on this side of the House suggested a short time ago that this was a "white elephant." To indicate the importance of this waterway to this particular district, I may say that last October owing to a shortage of surplus water and consequent shortage of hydro-electric power local plants had to be closed down alternate days for about two weeks, which entailed a loss of nearly a million dollars, to the people of Peterborough alone. Thp only right which the Hydro-Electric Commission has is to use the surplus water going over these dams which is conserved by the various locks and dams in the whole system. That is an important feature, but it is only an incident, because the Government is required under its agreement with the province of Ontario and its agreement with the Canadian General Electric Company to keep those waters at a certain fixed level for navigation purposes so that the power users may avail themselves of the surplus waters conserved during the summer months. So if these dams and locks leak the navigation level will not be maintained, there will be no surplus for power users, and consequently the Dominion Government will be liable in damages.

What is the amount of power produced on the Trent Valley
system?

One hundred and
twenty-five thousand horse-power.

The hon. member
spoke about works for the general advantage of Canada. Well, the committee is aware that many railways are being built in the West which are supposed to be for the general advantage of Canada.

But they are not
being built.

The work which we are now considering is just as much for the general advantage of Canada as many other undertakings that have been proceeded with. When it is completed I am convinced that it will be worth many millions to Canada every year. It is bringing thousands of dollars to that district at the present time by way of tourists. I do not care whether we get a dollar through selling our wheat or from a traveller who comes here to enjoy himself; it is all the same thing. Hundreds of thousands of dollars are brought into the country on account of that waterway; there is no doubt about it. Hon. gentlemen laugh, but it is a fact that a large part of the revenue of some of the states of the Union is derived through tourists. If a larger amount had been brought into this country last year through tourists, the conditions of exchange would be better than they are to-day. This waterway is not yet completed; there are twenty or thirty miles to be constructed. When that is done I think the House and the country will entertain a different opinion of it.

Another way in which this waterway will be of benefit to the whole country is in the development of power. There has been 125,000 horsepower developed by this waterway so far. Hon. members will agree that this power development will be of great assistance in the development of the natural resources in that particular locality. In addition, there is a large saving in the way of fuel.
What revenue do we derive from the power which is being developed?

The 125,000 horsepower has not all been harnessed as yet, but the Hydro-Electric Commission have some fifty or sixty thousand horse-power under lease which was given to the Sey-

mour Power Company fifteen or twenty years ago. The rates were low at that time.
But at present how much do we derive?
About $60,000 or $70,000, from the fifty or sixty thousand horse-power.
Is it the intention of the Government to harness the whole of the power?
Yes. We have taken it up with the Hydro-Electric Commission and they are carrying on the development of the power.
Under lease?
Yes, there is no trouble about that. They did question our power to collect, on account of the Ontario Government's claim, but they have abandoned that stand and are now paying rentals.

What is the period
covered by the lease?
I would not say just now. It is quite a long time.

Since the last sitting of the committee on these Estimates I have had the advantage of consulting with the chief engineer of the Railway Department, and I have become convinced of the necessity for the repairs covered by some of the items included in this vote. The chief engineer reports that for several years he has declined the responsibility for any accidents which may occur as a result of the present condition of the dam. But in my opinion it was an error to begin such a large public work-a work which up to the present has cost the country about $20,000,000 and which will involve an additional two or three millions before it is completed to Georgian Bay. I do not believe that the traffic in that district and the benefit derived by the people in that vicinity justify the expenditure. Of course, if we harness and sell the power developed by the dams we might in the long run be repaid, but if so the leases will have to be on a much more profitable basis. I would urge the minister to take action to increase his rentals, because at present they are out of proportion to the cost of maintaining the dams. Of course, the leases at present operating will have to be maintained until they expire. But the committee was informed at the last sitting that new leases are made out at the rate of from four to [Mr J. D. Reid.]
six dollars per horse-power. I think that is far too low; the department should get more than that. It would even pay them to develop the power and sell it themselves. The administration and management of an electric power development is different from the management of a railway; once the dams are built and the necessary machinery installed to convert the hydraulic energy into electrical energy, the amount necessary for upkeep is comparatively small. Such a source of revenue would compensate the country for the expenditure involved so far in this public work. But I would direct the attention of the committee to another matter. Last year we were called upon to vote for Trent canal improvements the sum of $427,000. This year the amount for improvements is $515,000, so that these improvements, repairs and renewals of the works cost about half a million dollars a year. At the next session I would like the minister to be in a position to inform the committee what, in the opinion of the department, will be required for the whole of the renewals m years to come. It seems to me that it would be an easy matter for the minister to have his engineers make a thorough survey of the whole work so that the committee may be in a position to judge what the country is committed to. If we are going to spend half a million dollars a year on improvements alone, not to speak of construction and betterments, which are covered by other items, we should go further into the matter and see what we can do to derive greater benefit from that work, or at least to lessen the expenditure which the country is compelled to vote every year. I would like the minister to give us the assurance that this information will be forthcoming next year-or, I should say, next session; for I do not believe the minister will have anything further to do with the matter after the next election. At any rate next session I should like the minister to give us the report of his engineers as to the state of the whole system and what repairs might be expected to be included in or covered by appropriations of Parliament in years to come.
I shall be glad to give a full report.

Might I suggest, if this is
agreeable to the minister, that we should

take up the other item of Trent canal construction and betterments?

with this exception. This item is simply for the carrying on of improvements to the Welland canal. Are these new
bridges?
New bridges to replace old ones which have got into such a condition that they must be renewed. The amounts are small.
Is this for repairs-not for any further construction?

This is all for repairs
and improving the canal.
It is more in the way of replacements of already existing construction?
Yes.
I notice that this item is chargeable to income. With huge deficits on our railroads and no tolls on our canals, where is the income?

Repairs and renewals have always been put in as "chargeable to income." There is the other expenditure for capital where the work is in the nature of an extension. This method was started many years ago in order to keep separate capital account and the account for carrying on the operation of the canals. At the time that that account was established, there was a charge on all traffic through the canals, but that charge was done away with a number of years ago. This method of keeping the accounts has been continued so that there may be no difficulty in keeping the two forms of expenditure separate.
Seeing that there are now no tolls on canals, would it not be better to put this expenditure under a different head from that of "chargeable to income"?

There is quite an income from water-powers. Along the Welland canal, there are quite a number of water-powers from which quite a large revenue is collected, so that we are justified in putting this item under the heading of "chargeable to income."
What is that income?

The annual report of
the Department of Railways and Canals gives the details of every source of income. The rents, hydraulic and other rents, collected last year, amounted to $72,366.45 from the Welland canal and $5,461.67 from the Welland ship canal, or about $78,000.

As we voted last year $150,000 for improvements, and as we are voting $165,000 this year for the same purpose, what is the Estimate of the department as to the total anticipated improvements that will be required?

A wash-out or a storm or something of that kind might occur that would cause more than the ordinary repairs. This item is a case in point where a storm caused damages at Port Dalhousie harbour, which damage was unforeseen. It would be impossible to make such an Estimate as the hon. member asks.
Will this item of $165,000 put in good order the constructed part of the Welland canal?
It will put it in good order for the present unles there is another accident.
If I understand the minister aright, if there are no storms and no accidents, we shall have no item for improvements next year.
In the carrying on of the operation of each canal system, you must have repairs each and every year on account of the traffic through the canal.
Do storms get bigger in a year when an election is expected to be held?
Not this year.
What is the traffic on the Welland canal?
As given in the report of the Department of Railways and Canals, the total tonnage of freight moved through the Welland canal is 2,170,779 tons.

What is the total
revenue of all the canals?

I gave the revenue of the Welland canal a few minutes ago. The canals are free to vessels passing through them. I gave the revenue for water-powers, and that is practically the only revenue, with the exception of some small rents for leases of land along the canal.
Does the minister mean that after we have expended these enormous sums in constructing and keeping the canals in repair we get no revenue from them?
I mean that the policy was adopted about fifteen or twenty years ago that all the' canals of the Dominion should be free. We maintain and operate them free for the use of vessels passing through.

What is the idea of keeping them free? Why should not the Government charge tolls on these canals? If the policy of no tolls is good concerning the canals, why not apply it also to the railways? It would not make our railway deficit any bigger. Why not have free harbours? It seems to me there is absolutely no sense in this policy. Why spend millions of dollars in opening up canals and keeping them in repair, and not charge anything to the users? That is socialism and I wish to direct the attention
[Mr. Vien.a
of my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) to that. He is a Tory of the old school, and I do not believe he would approve of this policy. It is more than socialism, I do not think the Russian Government would adopt such a policy, of expending millions upon canal construction and maintenance, and then not charge anything to the users. .

I would hardly like to admit that that was socialism. This policy was adopted about fifteen or twenty years ago by the Government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and I believe it was the right policy.	I do not think there was any
socialism in it at all.
Not at that time.

The reason why it was adopted was to prevent the traffic from the West and other parts of Canada going by the Erie canal and through United States ports. The United States Government made all their canals free, and if we had .not adopted the same policy, the traffic would have gone via Buffalo anc American ports. That was the reason given for our adopting the policy then, and I believe the same reason still holds good to-day. I believe it is in the interests of Canada that we should keep our traffic on our own waterways.

I understand the minister's position. As Minister of Canals, he is in favour of opening up canals and keeping them in good repair so as to handle the traffic from the West. In his capacity as Minister of Railways, he is in favour of keeping up the port of Portland in the United States so as to get the traffic from the West. How can the minister reconcile these two policies? How can he as Minister of Canals come into this House and ask us as the representatives of the people to vote millions of dollars for maintaining these canals so that we may get Canadian traffic, and then, to-morrow or the day after, come into this House as Minister of Railways and ask us for money to repair the port of Portland in the United States? I do not think his position is very logical, and I would ask him to explain how he can defend both policies at the one time.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman does not understand this question as well as some hon. members who, like myself, live along the Welland canal. These

free tolls mean that we are carrying the wheat of our Agrarian friends down here free.

Let me give an illustration that has arisen in one of our committees. Montreal for the last three or four years has been depending for its fuel supply particularly on Pennsylvania coal. That is brought in by water; if it is brought in by rail, it is much more expensive. The freight'rate on coal by water to-day from Lake Erie ports to Montreal is from $2 to $2.25 a ton. Now with the enlarged Welland canal, which is being built, and which I hope will soon he finished, and with the St. Lawrence canal built, there is no reason why the boats that are at present carrying the fuel for the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific to the extent of 2,000,000 tons, up to the head of the lakes and also around to Georgian Bay ports could not also go to Montreal for the benefit of the Montreal people. The fuel is taken to the head of the lakes for twenty-five, thirty or forty cents a ton,-fifty cents was the maximum during the war. It is a distance of 900 miles, and is a four or five days' trip. Surely, if the canal was built, that boat could go to Montreal, even if it had to come back light, for twice the rate to Port Arthur or Fort William; in other words, for eighty or ninety cents a ton. There is a loss to Montreal to-day of $1.50 a ton on every ton of coal she gets.
That coal comes from the United States?

That is the difficulty. Nova Scotia coal is so high. They are asking $8.10 per ton for Nova Scotia coal delivered in Montreal, whereas it used to be delivered in Montreal from Nova Scotia for about $3 per ton.
In what way would the Welland canal cheapen the price of coal to the people Of Montreal?

It would cheapen it $1.50 per ton in this way. You cannot to-day take the coal to Montreal that we take on the upper lakes with ships carrying only
2,000	or 3,000 tons. We take the coal to the upper lakes in boats of 8,000 to 10,000 tons, because the canal at the Soo is large enough to accommodate them.
Where do these vessels come from?
From Buffalo, Ashtabula and other Lake Erie ports.
That reduction in price would be in favour of American coal as against Canadian coal. I had understood that my hon. friend was a protectionist.
I am a protectionist, and we are to-day paying 53 cents a ton in Ontario for the benefit of Nova Scotia coal.
Why are you doing it?
Let us face the facts. Nova Scotia coal is costing so much to-day that it cannot compete with American coal, even with the 53 cents advantage in exchange.
You prefer competition and an open market?

We prefer to protect our own industries, but we do not want to pay through the nose for it altogether. Coming now to the question of wheat, in which our friends from the West are interested, the question has been asked why these canals are free, why they are not paying a revenue. They are paying a revenue to the whole people of Canada, to every man who produces an article or a pound of goods in this country.
Those people are paying the revenue.

No, they are getting the benefit of it. The price of the wheat of the Northwest is governed by the Liverpool market, and the price the farmer gets is the difference between that market price and the cost of getting it there. If you reduce the cost of getting it there, you put just that much money in the farmer's pocket. So, if we put a toll on the canals, it would mean the farmer would have to pay that toll. I say, therefore, that these canals are to-day paying the people of Canada well. They are paying the producers, and the same thing applies to the manufacturers of the East. Their prices are governed in the same way that I have mentioned as regards wheat. If you lower the transportation charge, it is just that much advantage to the manufacturer and to the people of Canada. The people of England to-day are realizing that the closing of many canals that have been shut up by the railways is a great loss to the country. If those canals were still in operation the people would be better able to control1 the railway rates. This question of free tolls is of particular interest to Montreal, because the people of that city have

been losing $1.50 a ton on every ton of coal they buy on account of the lack of facilities to transport that coal.

This is an interesting
discussion and I am sorry that I missed the first part of it. I have listened to the explanation given by my hon. friend from Port Arthur (Mr. Keefer), and also to the lucid explanation given by the minister in respect of these charges, and the whole subject is very interesting. There may possibly be something to say for making no charges on the passage of vessels through canals like the Welland canal, where it is necessary to complete with rail connections to the United States ports. For, my part, I do not think that the argument is a very sound one. I think there is a good deal to say in favour of the argument that every vessel that passes through a canal should pay a toll, but in the case of the Welland canal it is true that something may be said on the other side. But I should like to know what on earth can be advanced in support of the argument that there should be no tolls on the Trent Valley canal or on the Rideau canal. The Trent Valley canal has cost this country, if my information is correct, about $20,000,000 or thereabouts, and we are asked now to vote thousands of dollars to keep it up. There are necessary repairs to be considered, wages to employees, and so forth; all these things must be taken care of, and they cost money. I should be glad if my hon. friend would give me his attention, because I want to ask him a question. I want to know why I, as a Manitoban, or a Western Canadian, should be taxed by this Parliament in order that some people living along the route of the canal should pass through with their motor yachts and pleasure boats, happy and content, free of charge.
You are willing to make a concession on the Welland canal, which is of benefit to you. Why should not the people of these other canals be given the same concession?
On your own argument the Welland canal is of general benefit to the whole of Canada.
Particularly to the western producer.	.

Not particularly to the
western producer any more than to the eastern manufacturer. My hon. friend knows that. If there are good and valid reasons why this Parliament should pay interest on a $20,000,000 investment, and

vote thousands of dollars a year to maintain the canal, and get no revenue from it, then I submit that there is a splendid argument in that fact for the completion of the Hudson Bay railway, say, to Hudson bay, and its operation at a loss of between $150,000 and $200,000 a year. One argument is as good as the other. We should endeavour to be consistent in these things throughout, and I respectfully suggest to the minister that he free himself from tradition and past customs which apparently are now binding him, according to his own statement, and break out on' a real business policy in the administration of the canals. I do think that it is altogether wrong that the whole population of Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, should be asked to pay taxes to support the Trent Valley canal if it is of benefit only to the people living immediately along it. And the same is true of many other canals. It is not a business-like proceeding at all, and I hope the minister will change his policy.

I can hardly agree that the Trent canal or the Rideau canal is of as little value as the member suggests. The hon. member takes the position that the Trent canal is good only for motor boats. As I stated on a previous occasion, in the Trent canal we have 125,000 horse-power developed, so that if we did spend $20,000,000 upon the canal, it was well worth it for the water-power alone.

Is this country getting
any benefit from that 125,000 horse-power?
Certainly.
How much?

We get a revenue of $60,000 from 50,000 harnessed horsepower which is used, and we should get a great deal more but for the fact that leases were granted ten or fifteen years ago at a very low rental. Some hon. members ask why we do not increase the rental. Well, we do not for the simple reason that these leases were given for a term of 21 years, renewable for two more terms, or a period of 63 years. We shall get a greater revenue, however, as they harness the remaining available horse-power. From the hon. member's statement it would appear that only motor boats go through the canal.
