I want to tell him that the Trent canal is of great value to Peterborough and other towns along its course, and the 50,000 tons of freight carried through it will increase. Now, if it is fair, as I believe it is, that there should be free

tolls on the Welland canal which is of benefit to all parts of the country, particularly the West, is it not fair that the people living along the Trent canal should have the same advantage?
The minister mentions the town of Peterborough. Is that the place where a storm occurred recently?
In February last.
Yes, but the storm did not do much damage at Peterborough. In any event, any damage done will be repaired at the next election.
Is the damage chargeable to income or capital?
It will be chargeable to capital.	*
Is this particular item for repairs?
Yes.

The member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), has given us a good example of his fairness in the argument he has advanced. He is quite willing to take everything that is beneficial to the West, but he is not willing to reciprocate in favour of the East.
I said nothing to that effect.

That is a perfect inference from his remarks. I wonder if he thinks that the consumer in the East derives as much benefit from free tolls as the consumer in the West? I will admit that the manufacturer in the East may get some benefit-
Not much.

-but probably little. The balance, however, is altogether in favour of the man in the West. The hon. member's argument is perfectly unfair and unsound. Does he think that the revenue, not only present but perspective, from the electrical power developed along this canal is not worth something? Does he not think that the great tourist traffic that has developed along that canal as well as in other parts of Canada is worth something? I am credibly informed that last year the tourists along the Trent Valley canal left over $1,000,000.
In the canal?

And I heard the
statement, made by a very responsible man at a Board of Trade meeting not long ago, that tourist trade in Canada was worth to-day more than the whole wheat crop of this country. Does the hon. member think that that is something not worth cultivating? Or does he think it can be brushed aside as being of no consequence?
The tourist traffic is not going to go by the Trent canal any more.
That is where you do not know what you are speaking about.
It will go by Quebec.

Last year, in the upper part of this canal, where they had to bring boats up by marine railways, thousands of boats came up even under such difficulties. When that canal is completed to Georgian bay we are going to tap one of the greatest sources of revenue, in the matter of tourist traffic, on the continent of America.
You cannot tap anything in Ontario for the tourist traffic.
We may not be able to tap their supplies but we can tap trade.
Put a pipe line through from Quebec.
Could the hon. member tell us where the Muskoka lakes are?

They are not on the Trent Valley canal, but I am not so shortsighted as to be unable to see something beneficial to the country even if it does not directly affect Muskoka. In that respect I differ from the hon. gentleman who made that observation. I say again, Mr. Chairman, that this project has a prospective value to Canada that this Parliament evidently has no conception of to-day. We already receive a revenue of $78,000 a year from the water-powers on this system alone, and they are not nearly all harnessed up yet. Furthermore, there are thousands of men in the city of Peterborough who are more or less directly employed through the agency of this undertaking.
At election time.

Not only
at election time but all the year round. I want to say further, that it is time to stop haggling across the floor as to what is

good for the East and what is good for the West; we must open our eyes a bit and see what is good for Canada. I persist, Mr. Chairman, in urging the Government to complete this undertaking. It has been in contemplation for, something over a hundred years. Both parties in this House are committed to it, and time after time, session after session, parliament after parliament, it has been discussed. It has not yet been completed, and until the work is finished the country will not derive'the full benefit from it that it should get once these vessels are able to run right through to the Georgian bay.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Arguments concerning the Welland and Trent canals would be much more in order under the item to be taken up immediately after eight o'clock. The suggestion now is that item No. 125 (Welland: Improvements, $165,000) be allowed to pass and that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) be allowed to reply when the other item is being considered.
No, it is six o'clock.

Would
the question of tolls and rates be open for discussion on the other item?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The entire question will be open in connection with the construction of the Welland and Trent canals.

Is the discussion
going on immediately after eight o'clock.
Yes.

Item agreed to.
At Six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The Committee resumed at Eight o'clock.
Canals-Welland ship canal, construction, $5,000,000 ; Trent canal, construction and betterments, $339,000.

Will the minister
explain?

Yes. This money is
to be expended on the Welland canal as follows: section 1, $700,000; section 2, $800,000; section 3, $1,500,000; section 5, $600,000. Then for gravel which we furnish, $78,000; sand $112,000; cement, $745,000; metal work for locks and so forth, $50,000; engineering staff, $325,000; [DOT] construction railway staff, $90,000. Contracts were let on these four sections prior

to the war, and on each a good deal of work had been done; then they were closed down during the war, but we started the work again to provide labour for returned men in that locality. We carried the work on for a couple of years on a cost plus basis, for the reason that labour, materials and supplies were so high that it was useless to call for tenders. Now we have decided to continue the work under contract if reasonable prices can be secured.
Mr.	CAMPBELL:	The	old	contracts
have expired?

We settled with the
contractors for work that had been done up to the time we cancelled the contracts.
Mr.	CAMPBELL:	Did	you	open up
those contracts or let	new ones?

No, we started on a
cost plus basis. It cost us a good deal of money to close up the contracts, and also to start them up again.
Mr.	CAMPBELL:	But	the	contracts
were closed?

They were closed and
the contractors settled with.

I ask this question
because I was told a few minutes ago those contracts were never cancelled.
They were cancelled.

When you started
again you did not start on those contracts but on a cost plus basis, a new basis entirely?

Yes, we resumed the
work that had been done under contract and not nearly completed, but we started it on a cost plus basis, and we are carrying it on that way at present. Last December we decided that as probably prices of labour, materials and supplies would be down this spring we would be justified in returning to a contract basis. Accordingly instructions were given to the chief engineer and his staff to prepare plans and specifications as soon as each section was ready to call for tenders. Tenders have been received for section 5, and we will accept the lowest tender on a contract instead of on a cost plus basis.
These tenders do not seem to have been accepted.
They do not need to be accepted if we close the work down or proceed on a cost plus basis.
Is there any reason why the work should not be closed down? It is altogether new work.

No. We expect to have the other two or three sections ready in a few weeks for tender, and if the prices quoted are reasonable we will let contracts for those sections. Answering the hon. member, there are several reasons why the work should not be closed down. It cost us a lot of money to close the work down during the war. Then we had to start it up again on account of the labour situation.
What year was that?
That was after the Armistice, I think in February.
Did not the minister find a great deal of difficulty in getting labour that year?

There has been trouble right along. To close the work down again costs money, and unless we protect the work that has already been done there will be earth shoves and extra expenditures will be involved in removing the earth and keeping the work in proper condition.
Have not other works in the minister's department been closed down in the last couple of years?
I will be very glad to answer the hon. member if he will kindly let me finish my statement. Of course, if he insists I am ready to answer him now.
No, that is all right.

Another reason for continuing the work is that when the canal is completed instead of twenty-eight locks there will be only five and vessels of a cargo capacity of 300,000 to 500,000 bushels, although they will be able to go through only a 14-foot draft, will carry very much larger cargoes than are possible through the old canal.
Where will they go to?

Down to Kingston,
which is only a day's run to Montreal, where the grain is transhipped. So that is also an advantage. I am sorry to have to admit it, but at the present time labour conditions are such that if we can possibly carry on works that it would be a loss to close down we should carry them on, and I may say that right in the Niagara peninsula to-day there is a lot of unemployment. Those are reasons why at all events these contracts where half completed should be completed at a time when great benefits
will be derived both during the course of the work and after its completion.
When shall we reap the benefit accruing from larger cargoes of grain going through this canal?
These particular contracts will probably take three or four years to complete.
I mean the whole canal.

If we like to spend the money and rush the work it could be done in three or four years, but it would take a larger amount of money each year than I think we would be justified in spending under present conditions.

How much money is
involved in the completion of each of these canals?

The original estimate
in respect to the Welland canal was, I think, $50,000,000. That is the total amount required to complete the work and make the canal of sufficient depth to accommodate vessels of nearly 25-foot draft and of a very large tonnage. The present capacity of the canal so far as wheat is concerned is for vessels of about 75,000 or
100.000	bushels; when it is completed vessels with a capacity of 300,000 or
400.000	bushels will be able to pass through the canal. I remember when the rate of freight on grain from Chicago down through the Welland canal was 20 cents a bushel, and at that time the vessels going through the canal carried only about 20,000 bushels. The government of the day decided to enlarge the canal so that it would accommodate vessels carrying 100,000 bushels, and it was then thought that that capacity would be sufficient for fifty years. However, it was ultimately found to be too small; a much larger capacity was required. The cost of fuel is the only additional consideration affecting the rate of freight when you have larger vessels. I can remember when, prior to the war, the rates were five and six cents a bushel from Port Arthur to Montreal. In my opinion, with the enlarged canal the rates from Port Arthur and Fort William to Montreal will go away down. From Kingston down the rate used to be about a cent and a half a bushel and the rate from Port Arthur to Kingston was three or four cents a bushel. Of course, during the last six or seven years the rates have gone up very considerably, chiefly on account of the war, with its accompanying increased cost of

tonnage and increased cost of operation by way of labour and fuel and other necessary supplies. I think that this year the rate is commencing to get back to normal, and I am in hopes that before the end of the present season the West will enjoy rates as they were before the war. The rates from Port Arthur and Fort William have been materially reduced as compared with those of last year. The last rate that I was aware of before this evening from Port Arthur to Montreal was eleven and a half cents a bushel, but my officials have now handed me a memorandum showing the latest rate to Port Colborne to be two to three cents per bushel and from Port Colborne to Montreal, six to eight cents. Several years ago the Government built an elevator at Port Colborne in order that the grain might be brought through our own St. Lawrence route at as low a rate as possible. Now% if we had the Welland canal in its completed state it should not take more than an additional half-cent on the Port Colborne rate to deliver that grain or traffic of any kind at Kingston, "where transshipment would take place. If wages and fuel were as they were before the war, the rate should not be more than the pre-war rate, one and' a half cents a bushel.
What would the rate be from Kingston to Montreal?

At present there is no transshipment at Kingston. Before the elevator was built all the grain that came through the St. Lawrence was shipped via the Welland canal to Kingston and there transshipped, but since the construction of the elevator at Port Colborne the large vessels have carried the grain to that port, where transshipment has been made.
That elevator will be of no use, then, when the Welland canal is completed.

No, when the Welland canal is completed that elevator will practically be of no use, except for local work in the district, of course, as an investment it will be worth something in that way. The Maple Leaf Milling Company have their large milling industry there, with an elevator of their own. They distribute a lot of wheat in that district, and probably the same would apply to the Government elevator. Now, in my opinion this expenditure is justified on the ground of the great advantage which will result through the completing of this work, first, to the
[Mr J. D. Reid.]
West, in having their grain transported at the very cheapest rate, and, second, to the East in respect of other traffic. Cargoes coming from across the ocean and destined for the West will go through the Welland canal, and the West will get the benefit of cheaper rates. It is evident, I should think, to those who are in the West and, of course, to those who are in the East that, from the time of the opening of navigation until its close, most of the traffic goes by rail and then across from Georgian bay ports through to Port Arthur or Fort William. The large vessels which are on the lakes can carry the freight cheaply, and the proportion of freight that goes all-rail is freight that can pay higher rates and probably freight that it does not pay to rehandle. But freight from the East should go in vessels right through by the water route, because water transportation is much cheaper than transportation by rail.

In order that the questions which I know are going to be propounded to the minister with regard to these items may be considered as neither factious nor sectional in character, it is, perhaps, well that the committee should understand the feeling that is pretty well disseminated over Western Canada with regard to the Welland canal. We feel, as regards the Welland canal, first of all, that you have started at the wrong end of the proposition, because you will have to revise your estimated cost of expenditure from $50,000,000 to probably $75,000,000 on account of the change that has taken place in the cost of material and labour; in the second place, that unless you have a system of canals along the St. Lawrence, you will still have to transship any grain which is brought down to lake Ontario and, in consequence, you cannot compete with the Erie canal. All that you are going to do by the completion of the Welland canal is to allow the grain to come down and go out by way of the Erie canal, thereby putting Montreal and Quebec interests at the disadvantage which will come from, perhaps, a generation of going in that didirection. More than that, until you have shipping coming into Montreal and cargoes being carried both ways, you cannot take your grain to Montreal. At present the grain goes to New York, as we all know, where it can get practically bottom rates to go out, and at Montreal it cannot get that; the shipping does not come to Montreal to take the grain out. Last year we had com-

plaints that ninety odd million bushels of our crop went by way of New York while a very small proportion went out by way of Montreal and Quebec. You will simply increase the disadvantageous position of our Canadian ports by the completion of the Welland canal before you make any improvements on the St. Lawrence to give you the full advantage of carrying the grain down to Montreal and Quebec for transfer in those ports directly to the ships. On account of this feeling, there was before six o'clock considerable comment which went off in a discussion that was, perhaps, not very pleasant. Accusations of sectionalism in regard to the matter were made. The criticism of this proposition is not wholly upon that ground. Perhaps I might admit this much, that the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Campbell) and myself, "who have been very much interested in the Hudson bay proposition, have been more or less disappointed in seeing forwarded propositions which are practically identical with that of the Hudson bay route, identical in this respect, that one of them is up in the air as the Hudson bay proposition is today; it goes out into a district that is a wilderness and it does not connect. We say that that is practically what the Welland canal is going to do and what the Trent canal is doing to-day. Those canals do not connect and they cannot connect for years so that through traffic may go on them. You will have to spend millions on those canals before you can get a service sufficient to justify any part of the expenditure. With that admission, which is, perhaps, more fair to my opponents in the matter than it needed to be, I want to come back to the first point that our opposition is neither factious nor sectional in character, but is because we sincerely distrust the manner in which the proposition has been gone about.

Before
six o'clock we were dealing with the questions of tolls, rates and charges. Certain statements were made which I take the privilege of disputing; at least, I hope to place before the committee a few facts and figures in regard to the tolls and rates. If we are going to continue allowing vessels on our inland waters to make whatever charges they please, we might just as well apply the tolls and take a portion of the money, because the committee can depend upon it that these vessels, until they are put under government control, will collect to the very last cent from the producer and the consumer in this country.
There is not a doubt in my mind, and I am more convinced than ever, that they are to-day and have been for years past collecting the very limit of what they can collect in connection with their charges on our inland waters. The hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) would lead the committee to believe that the price of grain is established at Liverpool. That is quite right; but it is also true that the producer in this country has to pay the rate of freight between his home town and Liverpool, and rates of freight, especially on our inland waters, are beyond all reason. Let me call attention to the position that was taken by the hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora. He gave the committee to understand that by making large expenditures of money, they would have decreased freight rates from the West. What has been the story of these rates for years past? It has been that, instead of there being a decrease the rates have been constantly increasing; they have been doubled, trebled and quadrupled, and this Government is powerless to control the vesselmen.
What is the freight rate to-day from the head of the lakes to Port Colborne? It is only two cents.

The
hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora asks the question. His minister just told the committee a few minutes ago that the rate was two or three cents. Does the committee think these vessels are not going to charge the three-cent rate? The committee can depend upon it that they will. But the hon. member did not tell the committee what the rate was to Montreal. The minister told us that the rate to Montreal had been reduced to 11 cents. It is true that last year the rates were down for a portion of the time when there was very little traffic, such as there is at present, to between 11 or 12 cents, but he did not tell the committee that in certain months of the year the rates were as high as 15J cents for the carrying of wheat from the West. How can a farmer in the western provinces expect, under existing conditions, to be taxed to the limit when he can get only a small amount of money for his grain? There is no doubt in my mind that the time has come when the Government should take action in this regard, and when we Should have Government control over rates, tolls, tariff agreements and arrangements of these vesselmen. The more money you spend, the higher go the

rates-that has been the story in connection, with these vesselmen for years past.
You say that you have control of the railways as regards rates, and the greatest howl went up in our country a little while ago when the Railway Commission increased the rates on our railways. I believe their action in that regard was an honest attempt on their part to make the railways at least pay their way. But what about this other great transportation system that is running alongside of this railway system of ours, that can double or treble its rates without any control being exercised over it? These vesselmen are charging the producer and the consumer the limit in this regard and I sincerely hope that before this season goes by, the Minister of Railways and Canals will see to it that some of the boats that are owned by the Government are placed on the lakes and put in a proper condition to be a competing factor in the transportation facilities on our inland waters. I do not wish to take up any more of the time of the committee. I appreciate the fact that we have to complete the Welland canal, but I feel very keenly over the fact that we are pouring money into these canals, harbours, rivers, docks and piers throughout Canada without our having a word to say in regard to what the vessel men shall do or charge. The vessels come up the canals and blow their whistles, and our men, paid by the people of this country, rush to open the locks in order that the vessels may pass through. If the canals need any repairs, we repair them. We are constantly doing this, and yet we have no control. I feel that the time is not far distant when we shall have control.

Did I understand my hon. friend to say that the rate from Port Arthur to Montreal was 15 cents, and the rate from Port Arthur to Port Colborne 3 cents? That would make it 12 cents from Port Colborne to Montreal.

If I remember rightly the statistics show that they carried the grain in the month of September last for a rate that went as high as that. I do not say that that was the charge all through the season, and I am quite satisfied that the minister is not in. a position to say that 11 cents is going to be the charge all through this season. He cannot do it;_ he has no power to do it; he is helpless, because the Government have no control over these vessels or over the

rates they charge. I think there is no question that the rate will be more than 11 cents before the year is over.

So far as the rates
last season are concerned, I can hardly believe that there was a rate of 15 cents. I wired the other day for the rates from Port Colborne. However, with reference to the rate I gave a few moments ago for the present season, there is no question that that is the rate, and that. 111 cents was the highest rate from Port Arthur through.
There are two ways in which we can control the rates. I am sufficiently interested in this matter to want to see the rates from Port Arthur and Fort William to Montreal, and vice versa, just as low as possible consistent with giving the' vessel owners a fair profit, and I think every man in the House will admit that an investment of that kind should have a reasonable return. Let me say to the hon. member that it was brought to my attention a few weeks ago that the rates were very high last year, and in order to see what the situation would be for the present year, I took the matter up with the steamship companies. I made up my mind that so far as the Department of Railways and Canals was concerned, and had power, we would see that the rates from Fort William and Port Arthur to Montreal, as quoted by vessel owners, were justified, and I took the means that have been suggested by the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) of stating that the Government had twenty or thirty vessels, of Welland canal size, that were built in inland waters, and that if we were to be imposed upon by any combine I would feel justified in asking the Government to allow some of these steamships to be used to transfer grain between Port Colborne and Montreal. But there is not a combine. The shipping is not all in the hands of one company. There are two or three lafge companies, each with a large number of vessels, competing for this traffic, and I take it for granted that those who are interested in shipping will feel satisfied if we can prove to them that the rates charged are not combine rates, and are not unreasonable.
There is another form of competition, which I mentioned last year, and in fact every year that this matter has been up. Large American carriers have the right to carry freight, and they do so, from a Canadian port to an American port. If they are wanting traffic, from time to time

they will load their vessels at Port Arthur and Port William, take the grain to Buffalo, where it is transferred to American elevators, and then a smaller Welland Canal vessel will take that grain from Buffalo through to Montreal without violating any international law. So you have competition in that way in opposition to the steamships operating on inland waters. The same thing, of course, applies to Canadian vessels. They can carry grain from an American port to a Canadian port, and then transship from a Canadian to an American port without violating any international law.
I want to refer for a minute to what was said by the hon. member for Neepawa (Mr. Davis). I think he said that it did not help when the grain came to Kingston. The hon. member, of course, understands that grain going from Port Arthur and Fort William to Buffalo and other American ports has probably 400 or 500 miles of canals to go through, and that the grain is carried in small cargoes of probably
15.000	or 20,000 bushels. If it can go in large quantities to Kingston, it is there transshipped and taken to Montreal at a cheaper rate in vessels of a capacity of
100.000	to 125,000 bushels, and it is only 160 miles, or less than twenty-four hours, from Kingston to Montreal.

Shortly before six
o'clock the hon. member for. Marquette (Mr. Crerar) complained about the expenditure of this money on the Trent Valley canal, which he said was practically in the interests of Peterborough and the Peterborough district.
I never mentioned Peterborough or the Peterborough district.

Well, that locality,
which is practically the same thing. I do not think the hon. member wanted to be unfair, and I should just like to point out to him that there is an institution in Peterborough that provides a market for hundreds of thousands of bushels of western grain, and that is the Quaker Oats industry. The Quaker Oats Company was induced in the first place to establish their plant at Peterborough on the ground of being able to get cheap power through the development of this canal. I think it was in 1912 or in 1913 that I went through that institution, and at that time they had a capacity of, and were running, 12,000 bushels of oats every day the year round. In 1911 their daily output the year round was forty cars, 188
and the bulk of that was manufactured from western oats. After their plant was destroyed in 1917, the Quaker Oats people practically refused to rebuild in Peterborough without an assurance from the Government that the Trent Valley canal would be completed. The people of Peterborough were uneasy at that time, and I remember going with the manager of the Quaker Oats firm to see the Minister of Railways and Canals. The firm took the position at that time that if they had a reasonable assurance from the Minister of Railways and Canals that the then uncompleted portion of the Trent Valley canal on the Severn river would be completed, they would rebuild their plant. Otherwise, they would not. They got that assurance.
In what way is the rebuilding of the plant dependent on the completion of the canal?

I understood from the manager that at that time they had their plans all ready to build barges to bring down through the Trent canal from the Georgian bay all the grain necessary for their plant. They still have those plans. Before the fire they had a plant with a daily capacity of about 40,000 bushels of grain. On the assurance of the minister that the uncompleted portion of the canal would be completed in the course of two or three years, they rebuilt their plant. Any man who cares to visit Peterborough can see the establishment.
Where did they propose to build the plant if the Government had not given that assurance?

They intended to
manufacture, as they are doing now, in Michigan, where they have another very big plant. Had this assurance not been given these people, Canada would probably have lost this great establishment. Mark you, the market for the Quaker Oats output is not local. The output of that plant, I have been informed, and I think credibly, is practically all exported to foreign markets. A few years ago one could see train loads of Quaker Oats billed for Belgium, Denmark, and other places, and while today the market may not be entirely export, a few years ago it was. This manufacture provides a market for western grain, and these people are prepared, immediately the canal is finished, to bring down through it all the grain they require. I have every reason to believe that when the Trent

Valley canal is completed it will be of benefit, not only to the city of Peterborough and the surrounding neighbourhood, but also to the country at large. Furthermore, as an hon. member said this afternoon before six o'clock, the development of that canal would bring millions of dollars into Canada in the shape of tourist traffic. A man can take a boat at New York, go through by way of the Trent canal and in a short time get to Chicago. A few years ago when the canal was opened, a couple of boats went from a wharf in Ottawa clean through to Jackson's Point on lake Simcoe. When the canal is finished right up through the Severn river there will be no difficulty in going right on to the Georgian bay and the Quaker Oats people will be able to bring all their grain down from the West at a cheaper rate than they can at the present time over the railway.

What draught of boats
will the canal accommodate?

From Peterborough to Georgian bay it will accommodate boats of from six and a half to seven feet draught. In any case, it is sufficient to accommodate the barges that would bring down the grain required. Now, there is no doubt that we shall be able to secure a very large amount of money from the tourist trade if the canal is completed, and if we can get a million dollars or ten million dollars of American money distributed throughout Canada I cannot see that it makes any difference whether that money comes through the tourist trade or otherwise.
Mr.- GORDON:	Remember, no truck or
trade with the Yankees.

Oh, well, we truck
and trade with them, and if they bring in good money we will take it; there is no doubt about that.

You have changed
your mind since 1911.
A convert at last.
I never stood in need of conversion along that line.

It is never too late
to mend.

Now, without taking
up further time-I know that the minister is anxious to get his Estimates through-

We have no doubt
about that.

I will conclude by
urging upon the committee the importance of completing this little section of the Trent Valley canal. Last year small yachts could go through to Georgian bay, but, of course, this section of eight or ten miles must be completed, and I strongly urge the minister to go on with this work and complete it within the next twelve months.

I was much interested in what my hon. friend from East Peterborough had to say, but I still adhere to the position I took earlier in the discussion, and I do so not through opposition to the interests of Peterborough or the surrounding districts. As a good Canadian I am glad to see the people in that section prosperous, but to my mind there is a very important principle underlying this expenditure. I am free to admit that in these expenditures in the past we have not followed a wise and sound policy. As regards the Welland canal and the question of tolls on vessels passing through that canal, as I said when speaking on this subject before, there may be some good reasons why vessels should pass free of toll. Personally, I rather incline to the opinion that this view is not sound. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways has argued that it is necessary to have vessels pass through the Welland canal free of toll in order that we may compete with the Erie canal from Buffalo to Albany. As a matter of fact, the Erie canal is scarcely used now at any time for transporting grain. I have been in the grain business a good many years. The company I have been associated with has exported a considerable quantity of grain during the last ten or twelve years, and I know that, as a fact, the Erie canal is not used for transporting grain from Buffalo to Albany.
Why?

Because it can accommodate only barges carrying five or six thousand bushels, and it takes so long to transport the grain that no one will ship it on this canal. Is it necessary, therefore, on that account, to maintain free tolls on the Welland canal? But assuming that this is to meet the competition of the Erie canal, then I would point out that it is intended to benefit insurance and vessel agents and other interests in Toronto, Kingston and Montreal. I have no fault to find with that, but let us put the thing on a fair basis. When we come however to the consideration of the Trent canal, it is in a totally different position.

My hon.. friend from East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith), and the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. McGibbon), have argued that this canal is of value because it develops tourist traffic that promises to amount probably to several million dollars a year. Well, I am rather at a loss to understand what tourist traffic can be developed through a canal that will take narrow boats of only six or eight feet draught. The scenery must be magnificent indeed, if it will attract tourists under these conditions. I rather fancy the average tourist, rather than . travel on a slow boat through a canql that will only accommodate vessels of six feet draughr. will probably take the railway trains and stop off at the points of interest which they pass. If the argument is sound and a justification for this Parliament voting millions of dollars to build this canal in order that a few hundred thousand dollars of revenue may be secured from tourists, then I would commend to Parliament-and I am sure that my hon. friend from Port Arthur will agree with me in this-that it would be a desirable thing to spend a few million dollars of Canadian money advertising the splendid tourist qualities of the Lake of the Woods. There is no finer beauty spot in Canada than the Lake of the Woods, but if I were to seriously advance to this House the proposal that Parliament should vote one or two million dollars to build hotels in that district, and provide the necessary equipment, in ordier that we might accommodate tourists from the United States I should be laughed out of court immediately.

I did not argue for a
moment that we should spend millions of dollars purely for the sake of developing tourist traffic; the hon. gentleman knows that very well. But the canal system develops millions of dollars worth of power; and there are hundreds of thousands of bushels of grain, perhaps millions of bushels, that the Quaker Oats Company would bring down from the West, from the grain fields of the hon. gentleman's own province, to the city of Peterborough, grind it up there, and so create a market for the grain of the western farmer. I spoke from that point of view, and also mentioned as a side issue that millions of dollars might be brought in by tourists who would not wait for slow vessels but would come in their own gasoline yachts, capable of running thirty miles an hour. If my hon. friend wishes to. see them let him go to that locality in another six
188J
weeks and he will see one of the most beautiful sections of country on the continent of America,-a section that attracts thousands and tens of thousands of people from the great cities to the south even from points as far distant as California. Apart from that I did not advocate the building of the canal for tourist traffic, and I do not want my hon. friend to put such words in my mouth. I did not make a statement capable of bearing such a construction at all. I say build and complete the canal for the different purposes for which it may be used-carrying grain, supplying a market for the grain of the farmers-yes, and a good market too when you consider that one institution is capable of grinding about forty thousand bushels a day the year round. It is worth looking after and worth spending a little money to give them a chance to do it. Then there is, of course, the great development of power. But the hon. member for Marquette would say: "No, we do not want you to bring your grain down in your own barges. Pay the prices the railways wish to charge you, and if that takes three, four or five cents a bushel more out of the farmers in getting their grain to the market, all right, let them lose it, but don't build any canal." Perhaps that is not what the hon. member wishes to argue but that is the effect of his argument. I am trying to advocate something that will be a benefit to the farmers of the
West-a distinct benefit to those farmers-

I am going to deal with
that.

-and at the same
time be a great benefit to the community through which the canal passes, and bring in people from the United States and other countries to spend their money in the Dominion.
I thought the hon. member from West Peterborough was going to ask a question rather than make a speech.
I beg your pardon.

However, it is quite all
right.
Not the speech.

No. The hon. member
has asked a question and I would be the last person in this chamber to endeavour in any way to misrepresent his argument. My hon. friend has also referred to the value this canal will be in transporting grain from the Georgian bay to Peterborough, thus adding to the market fneil

ities of the western farmer. Now the Quaker Oats Company have had their plant in Peterborough for quite a number of years, and I am well within the
9 p.m. truth when I state that the mere fact that there was a Quaker Oats mill in Peterborough has not been a factor of any consequence in determining the market value received for oats in Western Canada-not at all. I do think, and I do not want to misrepresent my hon. friend, that when lie argues that this expenditure is justified because it will enable the Quaker Oats people to haul their oats from the Georgian bay to Peterborough in order to grind them there, that this is scarcely a strong argument to advance for the expenditure of millions of dollars on this canal system, and the expenditure of hundreds of thousands of dollars annually to keep it up. As far as power is concerned it is very desirable to have a revenue from that source, but I understand that the total expenditure to date, on this canal, is over $20,000,000, and the interest on that alone probably represents a million dollars a year at the very least, outside the maintenance costs, which are very considerable.
The principle I wish to lay down, Mr. Chairman, is that it is not a desirable condition of affairs that the public treasury of this country should be asked to provide the maintenance costs of a canal that really can only benefit the districts immediately adjacent to#it. If that argument is sound for the Trent Valley canal, it is equally sound for any local expenditure elsewhere throughout Canada.
How does the hon. member square that with our expenditure for roads which the public can use free of tolls? Does the hon. gentleman advocate tolls on highways?

My hon. friend has not cited a good example, but a very poor one. Expenditure for roads is a local expenditure, and the people who benefit from those roads should pay the cost and maintenance of them.
Not always.

The principle that I have enunciated is absolutely a sound principle. That is the ground upon which I question the wisdom of this expenditure, and why I think it is not unjust to ask that some revenue in the way of tolls should be secured from these canals. When the matter of additional expenditure for the 
Hudson Bay railway was under consideration-
Would the hon. member be in favour of tolls on public roads?
I think the toll road is [DOT] an iniquity and always has been; but the toll road out in the country is a different thing altogether from this.

They are both high
ways.

The road just serves
the people of a local district and they should pay the expenditure-
Not always.

-and in this case also they should put up the expenditure. That is the principle I am arguing. We have the Newmarket canal, we have other expenditures of a similar character, and I maintain that it is not unreasonable to ask these local works to produce revenue to meet at least a portion of the outlays that are necessary to carry them. I might go back and cite another illustration. A moment ago I was about to mention the Hudson Bay railway. When the minister had his Railway Estimates up a few weeks ago I opposed further expenditure on that: railway this year because this country is not in a position at the present time to undertake the financial burden, and for the same reason I am quite consistent in opposing additional expenditures on the Trent Valley canal.
Now as far as the Welland canal is concerned I am prepared to say that, in my humble judgment, the whole project was ill conceived and undertaken at the wrong time. I am not nearly so sanguine as my hon. friend the Minister of Railways is that this vast expenditure-which will probably run into fifty or sixty millions of dollars before the work is finished-will bring anything like the benefits he anticipates. There are laws operating in respect to the moving of grain from Canada to Europe and, no matter how many canals you dig between Welland and Montreal, our grain will go out largely by New York, and largely because of the conditions that obtain in ocean insurance and ocean freight rates. When this country has a population of twenty-five, thirty or forty million souls you will have heavy European traffic to our own Canadian ports; but no ocean going vessel that can load from Newport News, Philadelphia, Boston or New York is going to come to Montreal or Quebec to take a cargo of grain to Europe. And

when the vessel is returning from the other side it is very difficult for it to find a cargo for Quebec or Montreal as compared with Philadelphia or New York. That is the real basic reason underlying this thing, and I am convinced that at the present time when the finances of the country are in such an unsatisfactory condition, when our revenues may fail by possibly $150,000,000 to meet the amount of money this Parliament is going to vote this session, these public expenditures are not well advised. We should be retrenching in every possible way, and I really think that these votes in that respect are open to serious objection.

The principle raised by my hon. friend from Marquette (Mr. Crerar) should be given very careful consideration by the committee- the principle whether or not the time has come when we should reconsider the position taken some years ago and place tolls on all our canal systems that would at least meet the expenses of operation. If my hon. friend would take that position, as I understood the hon. member for Dorchester to take this afternoon, I would be disposed to agree with him. But when he asserts that tolls should be placed on a canal simply because it serves only a particular section of the country, and that another canal that serves a larger section of the country should be left free, he takes a position that I cannot agree with.
I have not taken that position.

Then I have wholly misunderstood the hon. member. I understood his argument to be that because the Trent Valley canal served merely a section of Central Ontario, Peterborough and the adjacent district it was not a work that should be free of tolls.
Perhaps my hon. friend will permit me? What I stated was that I rather inclined to the view, that arguments against tolls on the Welland canal were not very sound.
Are you in favour of tolls?
Yes, I think I would be in favour of them. But the argument appeals with fourfold force to a canal like the Trent Vajley canal.

That is exactly the position I understood my hon. friend to take, that because the Trent Valley canal did not bear relation to a
larger area it should be specially singled out to have tolls placed against it. If we carry that argument to its logical conclusion, we would be forced to say that because any work of a public character, such as the construction of a railway, a canal or a highway, or a subsidy granted to a steamship company to carry mails and passengers between certain points, did not serve all of the people of Canada it should not be assisted in any degree by the Federal Parliament. If my hon. friend will take the Estimates contained on pages 38, 39, 40, 41, 42 and 43 he will find millions of dollars voted by this Parliament for purely local purposes in so far as they relate to the rest of Canada. I have sat on the railway committee with my hon. friend and voted for the construction of a branch line of railway in Western Canada that neither he nor I expect in this generation to earn the interest on the capital expenditure, but that was no reason why the railway should not be constructed for our fellow citizens in the territory to be served in order that they might have transportation facilities with the outside world. This session we have voted subsidies for steamships plying along the Gaspe coast to provide means of transportation for our citizens there; also a large sum of money to maintain a ferry service 'between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. It would be difficult to argue that either of the latter services was of any material benefit, for instance, to the people of British Columbia.
How would you get your fish from Gaspe?
Or your potatoes from the Island?

These
are all inter-related one with the other. The point I wish to make is that if we undertake to say that because a public work applies more directly to a particular locality than to the rest of Canada we are not going to have it carried on at all by the Federal Parliament, I do not know where we are going to land, for there are not half a dozen votes in this Estimate that are not more or less of a local character. Coming back to the question of canals, if my hon. friend feels that we should retrace the steps we took twenty years ago and place tolls on all of our canals, he may find support for his position, but even then I think he would find he was placing us, to say the least, not in a very dignified position. Just go up to the Soo and see what

would happen. Three-fourths of the boats plying through the Soo canals are Canadian, and they carry people from all over the world. The moment you place tolls on the Canadian canal what will happen? Every one of those boats will go through the American canal. Is that the position we would like to take of placing our boats at a disadvantage operating through Canadian waters?
Will the hon. gentleman allow me a question? Has he any objection to our mercantile marine sailing on oceans which we do not own without paying tolls?
That is a big question.

My hon. friend had better come a little closer home. So long as the United States canals are free, and so long as our shipping is so closely inter-related with that of the United States, if we place tolls on our canals we are going to put our shipping at a disadvantage, and we are going to take a position that, to say the least, will not be very dignified, as I think my hon. friend will admit. Personally I know nothing about the merits or demerits of the Trent canal in its relation to the country through which it runs, but if we take the position that because a work applies more directly to a particular locality than it does to the rest of the couiitry we are not going to support it, we will have to eliminate seven-eighths of these Estimates. It is only in exceptional cases that you can say that any of the items we are voting are of general advantage to the people of Canada. Perhaps the Welland canal is one of these exceptions, but I have no doubt there are people in some parts of the Dominion who will say that neither the Welland nor the Soo canal is of very much immediate personal advantage to them. But he would be a short-sighted citizen who would assert that for that reason these great highways of commerce should not be maintained and made as perfect as we can make them. We are building harbours and elevators on the Pacific and the Atlantic coast, which are not, it may be contended, of equal advantage to all the people in every part of the country, but nevertheless it is our duty as Canadians to construct and maintain those works, in order that we may better the conditions of our citizens as a whole.

The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) has referred to
	*
the Trent Valley canal as a purely local institution. I contend that such is not the case; it is a canal which will operate, with the natural waterways in connection with it, from Georgian bay to lake Ontario. The distance from Sault Ste. Marie to New York by the Erie canal is 1,094 miles, while the distance from the same point to Montreal by the Trent waterway is 687 miles,, the advantage in distance for the Trent route being over 400 miles. With the advantage of shorter distance there is the further advantage of greater speed; a double trip can be made over the Trent waterway in less time than a single trip via the Erie route. Members of the committee know very well what development resulted from the establishment of the Erie canal in the state of New York. The Erie canal is a considerable factor in export trade, but we say that the Trent canal will be a much greater factor in that connection by reason of its being on a more direct line of communication and cutting directly through at an angle from Georgian bay down to Trenton. Evidence was given some time ago before a Royal Commission at Peterborough dealing with the subject of transportation to show that the grain could be carried by the Trent waterway from Midland to Montreal for one and a quarter cents per bushel while the rate at that time from Peterborough to Montreal was about five and one-half cents per bushel. A number of commissions have inquired into and dealt with this question; experts have been called and have given their testimony, and these commissions reported favourably upon the completion of this canal when it was about one-half or one-third constructed. As the hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith) has said, the Quaker Oats plant has a capacity of 8,000 barrels a day; in [DOT] other words, they can send out and take in each day a train a mile long. It is entirely an export mill; the local business is practically nil. I think the hon. member for Marquette said that such mills were hardly a factor in the matter. Well, if we had not such mills as that, how would the grain from the Canadian West be milled and exported? Surely it is an advantage to have a mill of that kind in this country, employing large numbers of men, bringing about the development of cities where they are established and exporting the finished product rather than the raw material. There are two other large firms operating very modern mills. The Quaker Oats mill is said to be the most modern in

the world, and it is ready to do this milling if the opportunity is forthcoming. Then there are other considerations. A turning basin has been dredged in the river at Peterborough. A lift lock, the highest in the world, has been constructed there. Various governments from the time of Sir John A. Macdonald down to the present have expended moneys for the carrying out of this scheme and establishing this Trent waterway from Georgian bay to lake Ontario. So, how can it be considered an unsound proposal at this day, when we have arrived at the very last unit, you might say, of construction, the completing of the chain by making the connection between Port Severn and Washago? If the objection had been raised some time ago, it might have been a matter of greater import, but in view of the fact that all these moneys have been expended and that the canal is only partly useful because it is only partly completed, it seems to me that having regard to the stake that Canada has in this, the greatest of its inland waterways, the work should be completed with little hesitation.
The suggestion that it is local work is, I submit, entirely beside the fact. Peterborough alone does not benefit by the Trent canal. It is true that we benefit to some extent because of the fact that we are upon it, but the blast furnaces at Midland will be able to have their products freighted through on this waterway to the plants at Petei-borough and Belleville at a far cheaper rate than would otherwise be the case. It means something in reducing the cost of living to the man who buys his flour or to the manufacturer who may use metal products-and Peterborough and Belleville are both cities where large quantities of metal products are used in various classes of manufacture. Included in these manufactures in agricultural machinery, which goes out west into that territory dominated by the hon. member for Marquette, who, I think, has always been anxious to have low prices for farm machinery, even if it should become necessary to import it without duty from the United States.
I would strongly urge that this Estimate be not questioned, because it is of vast importance to that part of the country east of Toronto. If there is one Estimate that is of importance among those which are before us this session, it is this one. The work had not been completed because other works were considered more essential and now, in order to give the
waterway an earning power, it is necessary that the last link in the chain be completed so that we may have a canal that will carry freight from Georgian bay through to lake Ontario. I attended at Chicago a meeting of the directors of the Quaker Oats Company after the mill at Peterborough had been blown up and burned; I think it was in December, 1914. One of the reasons why the directors of the Quaker Oats Company decided to build that great mill in Peterborough was their expectation that the Trent canal would be completed within a short time. Mr. Robert Gordon, one of the directors of the Quaker Oats Company, and, I think, the vice-president and treasurer, said so; they expected to bring their grain down in barges from Georgian bay. It seems to me that with the opportunities there are for the building up of a great city at Peterborough; with the mills we have there, capable of doubling and tripling their capacity; with the money that has been expended by various governments, no question should be raised at this time when we are almost at the last stages of the work. I do submit that in view of these circumstances no doubt should now be thrown upon the usefulness of this great inland waterway.

Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to be placed in any wrong position by my hon. friends from East and West Peterborough. I have no quarrel with the city of Peterborough; I certainly hope it will thrive and prosper, and that the district in the vicinity will do the same. It may be that it is necessary to complete this expenditure. My suggestion was in the first place that it should be possible to get some revenue from these canals and save the country from the burden of voting tens of thousands of dollars every year to maintain them. So far as the Trent Valley canal is concerned I appreciate the optimism of my hon. friend from West Peterborough, but I assure him that it will be a long time before the Trent canal will ever be a highway for transporting grain from Western Canada to Montreal. The Erie canal, I repeat is not used for transporting gTain. If my memory serves me rightly it was built at a time when there was but poor railway facilities throughout the state of New York. The Erie canal to-day and for many years past has not been used for transporting grain, and it is an impracticable proposition to transport grain by barges where you have to go through open water. It may be that

there is some local traffic that this canal can serve.

Is there open water
on the Trent waterways?

You would have to
transship your grain when you get to lake Ontario again and put it on vessels. The cost of transshipping grain from vessels to barges and from barges to vessels is such that the proposition is not a practicable one.

They can go right
through the Trent canal and down the St. Lawrence canals to Montreal.

That is not a practicable proposition when you come to work it out. It has not been found practicable on the Erie canal. I am not going to take up the time of the committee longer. I have stated my views and I am obliged to the committee for the courteous manner in which they have listened to me. I wish to assure my hon. friends from East and West Peterborough again that I have no quarrel with the city of Peterborough.

I must raise my voice in protest against this lavish expenditure for objects which, although, perhaps, good in themselves, are not warranted in the present financial condition of Canada. I do not doubt that water transportation is an excellent thing for the country, but the question is: What can Canada afford? If we are falling behind on ordinary account, as I am sure we will find ourselves to be falling behind, it is simply madness for us to go ahead with great capital expenditures unless they are absolutely required.

Has the hon. member
ever seen the Trent canal?

I have never seen the Trent canal; but I do not need to see it; I have seen the map of Canada. Very often we find that a man ruins himself by building too large a house on his property; but what Canada is doing, I am sorry to say, is placing herself in the position of a man who is ruining himself by having too many roads through his property. That is the situation. We have increased in this country transportation facilities beyond the degree in which the country can adequately use and support them. We have to call a halt. I know it is always hard to convince those who live in the parts of Canada that are necessarily affected by curtailment, to see the

matter in which other disinterested people see it. But we are spending far too much money. This is not the statement of a partisan; it is the statement of every thoughtful person in Canada. We must call a halt. There are certain service! that must be continued; interest on the debt must be paid; pensions must be paid-
Militia Department.

Militia Department
Estimates should be cut in half, if not by two-thirds. Very severe cuts might be made in the Estimates of other departments without hurting the country as a whole, although such action may be disagreeable and, perhaps, to the disadvantage of certain sections of the country. The trouble is that a public work, like the tariff, is largely a local issue, and when we come to deal with the curtailment of public expenditures, somebody's ox is always being gored. But we have to take a nation-wide look at matters; and while we may treat these matters lightly, the taxpayers of Canada, who are feeling the burden of taxation more heavily than they have ever felt it before, will call any government to account, no matter by what name they may call themselves, who will not curtail expenditure. We must curtail expenditure. If the debt, and the interest on the debt, keep mounting year by year, taxes will have to mount year by year, and when you get the country up to a certain degree of taxation, those taxes have a deterrent effect on industry. No greater benefit can be given to the Canadian people, no greater step can be taken in the direction of sound reconstruction than diminution of public expenditure and diminution of taxation.
What is the total estimate of the cost of completion of the work on the Trent canal and on the Welland-canal?

To complete the Trent canal through to Georgian bay,-to make it a complete waterway,-it will take about $1,500,000. To complete the contracts that have been partially completed on the Welland canal, will take about $15,000,000 spread over about three or four years.
Does that include contracts already let-?

The present vote and probably a couple more votes will complete the Welland canal to this extent, that there will be only five full-sized locks, and ve?

sels drawing 14 feet of water will be able to pass through the Welland canal.
Does the minister mean that contracts already let and contracts to be let to complete the work will amount to $15,000,000?

No. The contracts that we are letting now will complete the locks where these works are being constructed. After that the only work to complete the canal will be dredging from where this work ends up to Port Col-borne, but no more locks will be required.
What is the estimate of the total cost of completing the Welland canal?

The original total estimate when the work was started, was about $50,000,000, and according to that estimate, it would take about $30,000,000 or $35,000,000 to complete the work, but it is hard to say whether conditions will come down to what they were prior to the war. I expect that as these works are carried along, probably a year or two, conditions will be about the same as they were prior to the war, and we will be able to complete the work for about $55,000,000 instead of $50,000,000.
How much is to be expended yet to complete the canal?
If the total amount is $55,000,000, it will take probably about $35,000,000 yet.

On April 11, this item came up for discussion and I asked the minister if the present contracts for this canal were given by tender. The minister replied that they were not given by tender, but that the contracts were let on a cost-plus basis. There are very remunerate contracts, and those who take contracts on a cost-plus basis generally get what we call " plums."

Was the hon. member in the chamber a few minutes ago when I gave an explanation in regard to those contracts? What I stated then was that those contracts were originally given by tender and that they were closed down after the war started. The work was started up again about two and a half years ago just after the Armistice on a cost-plus basis and it has been that basis practically until now. We decided that it was not in the public interest to call for tenders when prices of labour and materials were very high, but last December, in renewing the cost-plus basis contract, we notified the contractors that as soon as the plans and specifications could be got ready we would call for tenders and that the contracts would be let to the lowest tenderer. The first one we were able to get ready was No. 5, which is mostly dredging. Tenders were called for and contracts let for that. Two or three others on which the engineers have been busy since the first of Jartuary preparing plans and specifications we expect to have ready within the next two or three weeks, when tenders will be called for. The whole work will then be on a tender and contract basis, instead of cost-plus.

My point is
this: The other day, just after I had asked for the names of the contractors, the Minister of Justice got up and brought in the closure, so I did not receive an answer.
I am a little bit suspicious about these contracts. Will the minister give the names of the contractors who got the work on a cost-plus basis?
They were the original contractors.

The names,
please.

That is for section No. 1. Then there is Baldry, Yerburg & Hutchinson, an English firm; the Canadian Dredging Company of Midland.
Who are the members of the latter company?
There are quite a number in that company.

Is Mr. M. J.
O'Brien a member of that company?

Before the item comes to a vote, I should like to make an observation or two. I have listened with considerable attention to the arguments pro and con, particularly the arguments of my hon. friend from West Peterborough (Mr. Gordon). He put up a pretty strong case for the completion of this canal. I do not blame the hon. gentleman at all; I do not question the strength of his case at; all;

I have no fault whatever to find with his argument. In fact, if he has not mentioned certain local circumstances and local names, I thought his argument might have been used for the completion of the Hudson Bay Railway, for it was practically the same argument I put forward for the completion of that road. He laid particular stress on the fact that this was the last unit that was to be completed, and that then there would be a proposition which could show that it was some good. I pointed out to the House some days ago that the Hudson Bay railway was almost complete, that the dump was complete, that only a few miles of steel remained to be laid to complete the road. I argued from that standpoint that the road should be completed, but the House did not see it that way.
I think there are two points to consider in connection with the Welland canal and the Trent canal. First, there is the question of construction, and secondly, the question of improvements, repairs and betterments. I think the two should be clearly distinguished. A short time ago votes passed for improvements, betterments and repairs for these canals. I listened to the explanation of those votes given by the minister, and I was suspicious that perhaps the full amount voted was not really necessary, but after his statement that serious results would ensue if the work was not maintained in proper shape, the vote for improvements went through without opposition. But that is an entirely different matter from the vote for construction. I do not propose to argue the question of tolls; I do not know that it is particularly inorder at this time. I do not propose to argue against the Welland canal or the Trent canal propositions as not being of Dominion-wide importance. I do not propose to say that they are entirely of local interest. I do not propose to say that they will not ultimately pay and be of benefit to the Dominion, but I do say, as my hon friend from Brome (Mr McMaster) has pointed out, that the situation now is such that it is really time to call a halt. It is not necessary to go on with these undertakings at the present time, although it may be in order to take them up at a later date That is the very argument I put forward in connection with the Hudson Bay railway. The two propositions stand pretty nearly on all fours. I said at that time that I was just as much in favour of economy as any member of this House, 
and that if the Government did not have the money to expend on an enterprise of that kind at that time, they would not hear one word further from me in favour Of the completion of the Hudson Bay railway. I mentioned at that time these canals, the Toronto harbour works, and other things of that nature, to show that the Government had money to expend on enterprises which, to say the most of them, were of no more importance than the Hudson Bay railway. It would seem that the expenditure of money is to be localized, and that enterprises in the East, such as the Welland canal, the Trent canal, and others, are going to have money spent on them from time to time, and in large amounts, while work on the Hudson Bay railway, which is just as important, to say the least, .as these eastern enterprises I have mentioned, is promptly stopped; no more money is to be expended on it, and the present construction is to suffer deterioration and decay, resulting in a great loss to Canada each year.
As. I have said, I am not going to argue the merits of these projects at all. I do not think there is anything in the argument that the Trent canal or the Welland canal is going to be of material benefit in reducing rates on grain. In that respect the one will in a way work against the other. If the Welland canal is going to do that, the Trent canal will not, and if we have one of them, there is no particular reason for having both, although up to a certain point they may both help. But the particular feature to my mind is this:	Hon. gentlemen on the other side
put up very strong arguments for the completion of these works on the ground that they are going to help the western farmer; it is said that they are going to mean lower freight rates and higher prices to the farmer for his wheat and other grains. It strikes me that hon. gentlemen opposite are very solicitous for the interests of the farmer, but the peculiar thing is that they will not let the farmers say what they want themselves in the way of reduction of tolls or increases in the price of wheat. Some years ago the question came up whether we should have reciprocity or not. The western farmer wanted it; he said that it would mean a bigger price for his wheat, but the people down here said:
" No, you cannot have reciprocity, although it will give you a bigger price for your wheat. We will give you instead the Trent canal and the Welland

canal, and some other works we want to build down here." The same thing is being-said now. The western farmer says he wants the Hudson Bay railway, and wants some branch lines in order to realize a greater price for his wheat, and in order that the carrying charges may be less. But the eastern people say "No, you cannot have these things; we will give you the Trent and Welland canals. You do not know what you want." Now, we submit with all deference to the learned gentlemen of the East wtho have taken so much trouble to look into the affairs of the western farmers, that we have a fair idea of what we want, and we know that what we want is in the best interests, not only of the western farmers, but of the people of Canada generally.
My hon. friend from Muskoka (Mr. Mc-Gibbon) had a few remarks to make before six o'clock relative to the fairness or unfairness of the attitude taken by the West. Let me point out to him the exact situation. We do not want anything in preference to the East. We recognize the importance of the East, and we should like the East to recognize, to some extent, the importance of the West. A little while ago we brought up the question of the Hudson Bay railway. Did my hon. friend support it? Notwithstanding that it was on the verge of being completed, and not, like the Welland canal, an entirely new proposition just under construction a few years, my hon. friend opposed it. What did the western representatives say on the subject? Some of us said that we wanted the Hudson Bay railway completed because money was being spent on eastern enterprises [DOT] that were, to say the least, of no more importance than that railway. All western members did not take that view . The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) said that under present financial conditions in Canada he thought that further work of construction in regard to the Hudson Bay railway should be deferred. Now, some of the western men were willing to go thus far, and the rest of us urged the completion of the railway, because, as I say, we saw money being poured out like water on other enterprises of less importance or, at all events, of no more importance than the Hudson Bay railway.
The Government, we contend, should be fair. They should treat West and East alike. If they say, "We must have money for repairs and improvements on the canals, but in the matter of construction we will treat the East as we do the West,
and defer construction work on these two propositions until a later date, when conditions become normal and money is more plentiful"-if they take that view, we shall have no fault to find. That is a fair proposition, and if my hon. friend from Muskoka is impartial he cannot object to it. But he says: "You must not have any money for the Hudson Bay railway, but it is necessary that we should have a vote to complete these propositions." We urge that both the East and the West should be put in the same category; if there is money for one there should be money for the other, and if expenditures cannot be afforded for construction work in the West, then no construction should be carried on in the East. That is only reasonable, and we certainly do most emphatically protest against the unfair discrimination shown to western interests in carrying on these expenditures, when other matters of equal, if not greater importance, brought before the House are not favourably considered.

A few minutes ago I made a reference to the Welland canal and omitted to read certain extracts which I have here-I simply overlooked them. The comparison made in regard to that canal was probably too favorable because from information which I have received, and according to my own figuring, the new Welland canal will not only not be an advantage* to Canada but will be a disadvantage if it is completed before the canals on the St. Lawrence are finished. As has already been pointed out by an hon. member to-night this is a case of putting the cart before the horse-the St. Lawrence canals should have been completed before building the Welland canal. Were the new Welland canal completed at the present time the Americans would get

a greater advantage than they are able to enjoy at present. I have before me a pamphlet on the canal system and I will read a quotation therefrom. The excerpt I wish to read is as follows:
Enlargement of the Welland, then, will give the Americans the following important advantages :-
1.	It will admit to Lake Ontario this enormous fleet of upwards of 500 large American freighters, and extend to that lake the keen competition now so seriously felt by Canadian carriers on the Upper Lakes.
2.	It will increase the length of haul of these large American freighters equally with that of Canadian vessels.
3.	It will enable American freighters to load American anthracite coal as return cargo ninety miles nearer the mines than at Buffalo, thereby saving the rail haul on every westbound cargo to that extent.
Canadian vessels, on the other hand, will gain merely the increased length of haul in large freighters. The point of trans-shipment will be mo roly changed to Kingston Instead of Fort Col-borne, and our net gain will be simply the difference in cost of carriage between those points in large freighters, and in vessels of Welland canal size.
It is clear that under these circumstances, the chances of cargoes going through to Montreal will be materially reduced below what they are at present.
Another paragraph in this pamphlet says:'
Then again the main dependence for return oargo at Buffalo is anthracite coal. Oswego is ninety miles closer than Buffalo to Scranton, the centre of the anthracite coal district. vIn spite of the fact that large freighters cannot come down to Lake Ontario, Oswego already shipped about 250,000 tons of anthracite west in 1911.
The contention therefore is that if the Welland canal is finished at the present time it will be a real disadvantage to Canada. I have been told that by engineers, by those who are in the transportation business, and by others who claim to know the conditions. On the face of it their contentions appear to me quite reasonable and for that reason, as well as for the other reasons I have mentioned, this item should not be allowed to pass.

Before this item passes I wish to add my protest to those which have been heard from this side this afternoon and this evening. It strikes me that before entering upon any such large expenditure as this, we should look at the financial and economical situation of the country, because if not bankrupt we are very nearly so. We should therefore scrutinize in the closest possible way every expenditure. It must be shown, and shown conclusively, that the moneys voted for the Trent canal and for the Welland canal
are absolutely necessary and 10 p.m. that an emergency exists, that they should be completed in order that some immediate and practical benefit may result therefrom; that we are expending this money in order to preserve the advantages derived from the expenditure already made. For my part I must say that I oppose this expenditure. With all due deference to my hon. friends from East and West Peterborough, and to other hon. gentlemen, I would advise them to do as a large number of members on this side-and I presume some hon. gentlemen opposite have done-that is to pass for themselves a kind of self-denying ordinance with regard to public works. We have been told very frequently by ministers and others that if the ministry feels itself free to carry on these public works it is largely on account of the pressure brought to bear by local members or by people from the particular district concerned. Take the case of the members from the district of Quebec. There are large public works that remain to be carried out in that district. We have the pledge of this Government, as well as of former governments, that these works should be constructed but by a species, as I have already said, of self-denying ordinance we have refrained from using our undoubtedly great influence with the Government and pressing our views on them. Had we wished we would have kept this House in session for very long periods of time and, I think, we could have succeeded in convincing members generally that these works in our district are of urgent public importance and should be completed. I think the same is true to a considerable extent, of works in other parts of the country: but the hon. members in question have refrained from pressing their claims, they have refrained from endeavouring to make political capital, they have refrained from endeavouring to get certain advantages for their constituencies, and it seems to me therefore that the Government should very carefully scrutinize such items as this before embarking upon expenditures. For example, there are in our district what is known as the St. Charles river works upon which over $2,-000,000-I think the figures are correct- have been expended.
