These works are now going to. ruin because the money necessary to conserve them-perhaps two, three or five thousand dollars-is not being spent. They are going to ruin, thus entailing the loss of the large sum that has already been

spent; the Government is allowing these works to deteriorate, to be carried away by the tide and so on. If the Government is carrying economy to that point in one section, surely it should not embark upon any new or expensive undertaking in any other part of the country. Personally I have no wish to lay it down as a broad principle that we should not undertake certain public works, and should not construct canals. Canals had their use in days gone by. I have no doubt that, in the early days of Confederation, canals were absolutely necessary for transportation purposes in this country, and perhaps it may be shown that they are of some utility. But they are not of such immediate practical utility that we should continue to operate them in view of our present financial condition. I think, therefore, the minister will be well advised to cut the amount necessary to spend on these undertaking to as low a figure as possible.

If'consistency was one of the virtues of the Minister of Railways, I would tell him how much he has sinned against it since the introduction of the items which refer to canals and other public works. But it is said that if a sin is committed twice it appears a sin no longer, and I am afraid that the minister has sinned so frequently that he no longer attempts to be consistent. A few weeks ago he submitted to this House an appalling statement in respect to our national railways and he said, "I am sorry, but I am obliged to ask the indulgence of the House. I have a deficit of $70,000,000, and I hope that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House will help me in finding some solution for this great difficulty in which I find myself." Many suggestions were offered, including a suggestion that he retrench and economize, but to-night the hon. gentleman is launching the country into another undertaking which will involve in the near future an expenditure of $55,000,000. What will be the benefit? Very slight indeed, Sir, if any. In fact, there are some persons, presumably well posted, who say that any benefit will be derived by Americans much more than by Canadians, while others say that the expenditure involved will be out of all proportion to the benefit which will accrue. But more than that, the hon. gentleman is creating a new competitor for his railways, and will have a still greater deficit to meet. It has been pointed out to him on several occasions that full advantage is not taken of the Transcontinental railway 
for the transportation of grain. When the policy for the building of that railway was introduced in this House in 1903 it was argued that such a railway would enable western wheat to be shipped through our Atlantic ports and would materially reduce the cost of transportation from Winnipeg to the seaboard, very much to the benefit of the western provinces and - of the eastern seaports. Further arguments in support of the construction of the Transcontinental were that it would give a shorter route between Winnipeg and Quebec and that the very low maximum grade of .4 of one per cent would give a hauling capacity of 1,780 tons as compared with only 940 tons on other roads. Well, Sir, the Transcontinental is in operation, hut the Minister of Railways has not seen fit to take full advantage of it. Has he tried to divert the transportation of western wheat to our Atlantic seaports? Not at all. On the contrary, he has done his best to prevent it. It has been shown that at present the rate of transportation of wheat from Winnipeg to New York is 32 cents a bushel, as against a possible rate over the Transcontinental from Winnipeg to Quebec in summer and to St. John, N.B., in winter of 17 cents a bushel. I understand that this has been brought to the attention of the minister, but without avail. It has been shown that with the low maximum grade of .4 of one per cent a trainload of sixty cars, each of a capacity of 1,000 bushels, or 60,000 bushels, could be hauled along the Transcontinental railway. The Government reports show the per train mile cost for a loaded freight train of 260 tons in 1905, when this policy was decided upon was $1.21; in 1913, the year preceding the war, it was $1.60; and in 1918, when the war was over and the cost of wages and fuel had greatly increased, the cost was $2.49. So that in the thirteen years the cost per train mile had increased 100 per cent, or about 8 per cent per annum, and the load carried per freight train had increased 75 per cent. The figures for 1920 are not yet available, but if the increased cost were in the same ratio, 8 per cent per anum, or 16 per cent additional for the two years, it would make a total cost per train mile of $2.90. But in 1920 a considerable increase in wages had to be allowed to conform with the wage scales in the United States, so if another forty per cent per train mile be added to cover this the cost would be $3.30. Assuming that loads could be found for only one-fourth of the cars re-

turned to Winnipeg, the cost of hauling back the other three-fourths empty would have to be added, and the figures would then stand as follows: 50 cars at $3.30 per train mile, $4,455; cost of hauling three-fourths of these cars empty-and an empty car is one-third the weight of a loaded car, but say 40 per cent-it would take 40 per cent of the cost of hauling the loaded cars to Quebec to haul back three-fourths of the cars empty to Winnipeg, or 30 per cent of $4,455-$1,336. That gives a total of $5,791 as the cost of hauling 60,000 bushels of wheat to Quebec and hauling back three-fourths of the cars empty, or 9.65 cents, in round figures 10 cents per bushel. Then, 30 per cent, or three cents, may be added for profit for the railway, making the cost 13 cents. Something might also be added owing to the fact that a train of fifty cars of wheat would weigh much more than the average train figured on in the Government report. Adding on this account 30 per cent, or 4 cents per bushel, the total, 17 cents per bushel, would seem a profitable price for the railway for hauling wheat from Winnipeg to Quebec. At present the rate from Winnipeg to New York is 32 cents a bushel by water and rail while the rate from Winnipeg to Quebec is 36 cents. So that at 17 cents a bushel the Canadian Government railways could transport western wheat from Winnipeg to Quebec, thereby competing with other lake and rail routes from Winnipeg to Montreal and to New York. These figures are absolutely reliable. They are based on data furnished by officials of the Transcontinental, and are in accordance also with figures furnished by the Interstate Commerce Commission with respect to the cost of hauling trains per train mile on the large American roads under state management-which, as is well known, was an expensive management. The rate on grain from Georgian bay ports, Midland to Halifax, for example, a distance of 1,215 miles, is 21.17 cents per hundred pounds or 12.7 cents per bushel. This information will be found in the tariff of the Grand Trunk, item 467. This rate applies over a variety of grades, sharp curvatures, congested track, expensive terminals, and, at present, two systems. If the same basis were applied from Winnipeg to Quebec, a distance of 1,350 miles, the rate would be 14 cents per bushel over a non-congested, straight, low grade track, which is now idle. This would save shippers the extra elevation, handling and incidental grain losses at the lake ports, also any extra for the rail haul Winnipeg to Port Arthur, and most of the charges across the lakes. The Transcontinental would become the saviour of the country. It would become the saviour of our Canadian National railways instead of being such a burden to them. The St. Lawrence route would be greatly strengthened and Canadian grain would reach the seaboard at less cost than by other routes-which is very necessary in view of present conditions.
What is the date of that?

February 3, 1921. At present, Sir, we have a good rail system of transportation in the Transcontinental and our other national roads. But will the minister listen to such a proposal? Not at all. He has invited suggestions from all quarters, but when constructive suggestions are made he does not listen to them. He invites the House to vote additional sums of money for public works which will mean an expenditure of some $50,000,000 or $55,000,000 and which will create a big competitor of the Canadian National railways, with resulting benefit not to Canada but to the American seaports. I think the committee will be interested in knowing something about the quantity of wheat transported through American ports during the last six years. If I understood rightly the member for Marquette, he said that very little western wheat was sent through American ports.
Oh, no; he put it the other way.
I am glad to accept the correction; I misunderstood him. I could not understand how he could make such a statement, in the light of the information that I have before me.
What is the name of the pamphlet that the hon. gentleman is quoting from?

I was quoting from the data contained in a memorial to the Railway Commission of Canada by the Quebec Board of Trade and the Quebec Harbour Commissioners. I am sorry that the minister, who has had all that information before him for some time, has not given it more attentive consideration. As I have said, he invited suggestions, but when they are put forward he disregards them. Not only does he do that; he creates competitors whose operations would increase

the deficit which the national railways have suffered in the past and involve the country in large expenditures of money. Hon. gentlemen will be interested to hear that in the years from 1912 to 1918, 1,906,000,000 bushels of wheat were shipped from Fort William by water, of which 577,000,000 bushels went through Canadian seaports and 518,000,000 bushels to Buffalo and thence, the greater part of it, to New York, Philadelphia, and other United States seaports. Rates are so arranged on the American railways and canals that they compete with the Canadian railways, and the Canadian railways are occasionally obliged to take a loss. At a hearing held by the Board of Railway Commissioners in February last it was stated by the traffic manager of the Canadian Pacific Railway company that they were losing money on the present rates from the bay ports to Montreal or St. John, but that they could not help it; that if they did not meet the competition the whole of the wheat traffic would go through American ports. I have serious doubt how they managed the figures to establish that they take a loss in the transportation of the grain. I do not believe that a railway as well managed as the Canadian Pacific would continue in such a trade if they were losing money. But as regards our Canadian National railways, we built the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific from the western coast to Moncton, New Brunswick, especially for the purpose of carrying western grain. When those roads were commenced, the strongest arguments in favour of construction were the shortening of the transportation from Winnipeg to the seaports, the reduction in grades and the grater hauling capacity that trains over that line would have. When the roads were completed, one would naturally think that the Government would take advantage of them. They did not;, they did not give rates which were well within the figures which I have shown. At present the rate from Winnipeg to Quebec is 36 cents a bushel, when it could be as low as 17 cents, but the rate could be 24 or 25 cents and still be seven or eight cents lower than the rate to New York by lake and rail. Moreover, when the Board of Railway Commissioners sat in Quebec, we put this direct question to the traffic managers: "Why do you not give to Quebec the same rate that you give to New York and Montreal?" Quebec, I might say, was on a different rate altogether. They replied: "Well, there is no competition; there is no other route; there
[Mr. Vien.J
is no other railway; there is no other transportation facilities to Quebec, whereas, in Montreal we have to compete with the American canals; once the grain is in Quebec, there is no competitor." I say: Yes, there is a competitor; the competitor is the Transcontinental railway; but the competitor is not alive to the advantages which nature and the construction of that road, under the conditions under which it was constructed, give to it. When we put this other question: "Why do you not use the Transcontinental railway?" and when we showed to those traffic managers the figures and asked them why they should not reduce their rates on the Transcontinental railway so as to compete with New York and other American ports, they said: "We (cannot do that; if the Transcontinental were to do that, it would put all the other railways out of business," meaning thereby that Quebec, when there is no other competitor in the field, can be charged a higher rate; but when there is a competitor, we cannot take advantage of the competitor, because if we were to do so, we would put the other railways out of business. In 1903, in 1904, and all the time that the Transcontinental and the Grand Trunk Pacific were under construction, we knew that the road would be some 250 miles shorter between Winnipeg and Quebec than the route over the Canadian Pacific between Winnipeg and Montreal. We knew that the grades would be better; that transportation by that route could be much cheaper and would compete successfully with the lake-and-rail route and other railways. But now the Canadian Government will not take advantage of that; they will not use the Transcontinental railway to the best advantage to which it could be used, because if they did so, it would put some other railways out of business. The Government of Canada have onex duty to perform which is to see that the affairs of this country are managed in a business-like way.
Let us take another condition. Supposing that the Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk were to-day in the position of the Canadian National railways; supposing they had a line in the same situation and condition as the Transcontinental railway. Would they hesitate for one moment to compete with the Canadian Government road? Of course they would not. They tell us themselves that they are obliged to meet competition in Montreal with American roads and American canals. If the Canadian Pacific owned the Transcontinental railway and were able to give

better rates, they would not hesitate for a moment to give better rates and to take advantage of the better situation which they would have. The Canadian Government are by no means justified in not taking advantage of the position they occupy. By diverting to Canadian ports over the Transcontinental railway the traffic of Western Canada, they would attain two great advantages for this country. They would reduce the cost of transportation of western wheat to the great benefit of the western farmer, and they would increase traffic over the Canadian National railways.
Another objection which we met before the Board of Railway Commissioners was that the grain went to New York because there tramp vessels in any number could be found. We have now a complete fleet of Canadian Merchant Marine, and the Canadian Merchant Marine could be used to no better advantage than to help the Canadian National railways in getting out of the muddle in which they are at present. Surely we have all the tramp vessels that we need, when fifteen or twenty of them are anchored idle in the harbour of Halifax, and when others roam over all the seas in quest of freight and cargoes. We have the cargo-it is the western wheat. We have the railway-it is the Transcontinental. We have the tramp vessels-they are the Canadian merchant ships. With a complete system of that character, we should be able to help the western farmer to reduce the cost of his transportation and the Canadian National railways to increase their traffic and thus reduce the annual deficits which are such a burden to the country. I wish the Minister of Railways would be consistent and would endeavour to accept the suggestions that he so cordially invited at the opening of the session, but which he is so reluctant to follow when they are put forward.

I have listened very earnestly to many arguments that have been put forward as to the reason why this Trent Valley canal should be gone on with. The hon. member for Peterborough East (Mr. Sexsmith) stated that this was necessary for conservation purposes. If that be a fact, again it becomes purely a provincial matter, because hon. members of this committee know very well that the natural resources of Ontario belong to that province. If the people of Ontario wish the canal for conservation purposes, then it is up to the provincial Government to construct it.
Another argument was put forward that the construction of this canal was necessary
in order to provide cheaper transportation of grain for the western farmer. Again our eastern friends are very kind to the western farmer in endeavouring to provide cheaper transportation for his grain. I am at a loss to know what system of waterways we are going to have. The Minister of Railways is talking about constructing the Welland ship canal and continuing it down to the port of Montreal, making of it a deep waterway system. Then this Trent Valley canal is going to be part of what is known as the Georgian bay canal.
The Trent canal and the proposed Georgian Bay canal are two entirely different works.
I accept the minister's correction, but the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Gordon) made the statement that this canal had to be continued up to the Georgian bay.

The Trent canal extends from lake Ontario to the Georgian Bay ports. There has been about $20,000,000 spent on it, and about $1,250,000 or $1,500,000 is still required to complete the western end. Then it will be a through waterway from the Georgian Bay ports to Montreal.
That will be a third waterway system.
No, only two. The Trent canal will be a complete system, and then there will be the Welland canal. The Georgian Bay canal has not been started at all.

That is in
prospect.
It has been there for thirty years.

Another argument made was that the Quaker Oats people would .not reconstruct their plant that had been destroyed by fire unless they received an assurance from the Government that the canal would be maintained, and that they would be given cheap electric power. ,
. Hon. Mr. REID: I wish to correct the hon. member. I never made the statement that there was a pledge given to that company that they would get cheap electric power. We are not selling power.

I did not
attribute that statement to the minister; it was made by an hon. member of the House. Now, if the Quaker Oats people

wish to go into the business of manufacturing foodstuffs for export, and that is their sole object, their best plan, it seems to me, would be to get nearer to the field where their raw material is produced. They could also get cheap power there, on the Lake of the Woods, where there is already situated the Lake of the Woods Milling Company, a very large concern manufacturing foodstuffs for export. So that argument is knocked on the head
The only argument this committee can entertain is that the Federal Government got its head into a noose held by the Provincial Government of Ontario, and that the Federal Government is practically bound to keep this canal in repair in consequence. All other arguments fail.
My hon. friend from East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) made the statement that members on this side of the House were finding fault on the ground that this was purely a local matter, and for local benefit. I maintain that that is correct. He instanced a case on the Atlantic sea coast where ships were receiving subsidies to provide transportation for settlers along that coast which they otherwise wouild not be able to get, and he asked what benefit that was to the people of British Columbia. If he will look through the Estimates he will find at page 46 that the same thing obtains along the Pacific coast. Large subsidies are being granted to ships along the Pacific coast. There is one item, for instance, of $130,509 for steamship subsidies, another for $21,000 for a steamship service between Prince Rupert and the Charlotte Islands, another item of $3,000, another of $25,000 for a steamship service between Victoria, Vancouver and Skagway, another of $24,800, and another of $5,000-all on the Pacific coast. We do not complain that these subsidies are granted to provide transportation facilities along the Pacific and Atlantic coasts; not at all, the people have to have means of transportation. But on this little stream, a dry creek, you might call it, on this Trent Valley canal, we have already expended $20,000,000, and year after year we are asked for a further grant of $500,000; when we are asked to expend $5,500,000 on the Welland canal, at a time when, as my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) very well put it, we cannot afford to spend such lavish amounts of money. It has been said by big business men of Canada that the Government is spending money like a drunken sailor, and we have an example of it here to-night.
TMr .T. D. Reid.]
It is also said that these canals will cheapen transportation rates. I am sure that the minister knows that the more this Government spends on our inland waterway transportation system, the higher the rates become. I would ask my hon. friend if he would be willing, as Minister of Railways in this Government, to introduce into this House a Government measure to bring the ships on our inland waters under the control of the Board of Railway Commissioners, so that we would have some control over their rates in view of the fact that we are spending so much money in aids to navigation. There is no answer. Mr. Chairman, I am opposed to the passing of this item, and I shall vote against it.

I suppose it will seem rather strange for a Western Ontario man to oppose the expenditure of public money on the Welland canal, yet I am opposed to it for this reason:	Some weeks ago
when the resolution was under discussion dealing with the construction of a great waterways system all the way down the St. Lawrence, I opposed that on the ground that the country was not financially capable of undertaking that enormous expenditure. To complete that great waterways system would require no less a sum than $600,000,000 or $700,000,000. The Welland canal is simply a link in that chain of waterways, and will be of no practical use unless the rest of the system is completed. In my opinion it is utterly impossible for this country to undertake at this time the expenditure of such a sum of money as $600,000,000 or $700,000,000. It has even been contended, and with considerable force, that the completion of the Welland canal before the completion of the other links in the great waterways system will be a detriment to Canada rather than of assistance. If that is the case, we have an additional reason why we should not vote this $5,000,000 at this time. If the completion of the Welland canal without the completion of the whole system is not going to be of any value to the country, we should not enter upon the expenditure of another $50,000,000 which will be required in order to comple that one link. We would at least save the interest on that sum of money, which would amount to between two and three million dollars a year, and that is very well worth saving at the present time, especially in view of the fact that we have no revenues from these canals whatsoever. Last week, I think it was, while we were discussing some other Estimates, I ex-

pressed the opinion that the canals of Canada should be made self-sustaining. I find there are now some voices raised in support of that contention.
As for the Trent Valley canal, I have seen it, and it seems to me it is after all only something in the nature of a glorified Newmarket canal. It is never going to be of any very great benefit. I do not imagine that the commercial traffic that will ever pass over that cana'l will amount to anything at all. It is practically negligible, and while I can quite understand the solicitude of the hon. member for West Peterborough (Mr. Gordon) for this project, as a Canadian who desires to see the moneys of the country expended properly, I cannot support it. I think the item should be struck out altogether, so far as capital expenditure on this undertaking is concerned. In the present position of the country, it is quite unjustifiable for the Government to go on with the construction of permanent works in connection with the Welland or the Trent canals, and I therefore move that the item of $5,000,000 for the continuation of the work on the Welland canal be struck out.

I can hardly believe that the hon. member is sincere in moving a motion of that kind. This item is absolutely necessary, for the reasons I have stated on several occasions. This work was started before the war, after it had been considered, not only by this Government, but by previous governments, and by both parties. Both political parties agreed that it was a work of necessity and one that would be advantageous to all parts of Canada. It was commenced, and a great deal of work was done. To abandon the project now would be to do a great injustice to all parts of the country, and it would simply be throwing away money that had already been expended.
I have not been able to hear the minister. Is he speaking about the Hudson Bay railway?

No, I referred to that a short time ago, but I will take it up again when we come to that subject. My hon. friend (Mr. Euler) may not think this work of any value to his own district, or to the rest of Canada. If so, I suppose he is right in moving the motion; but I cannot agree with him.
It is not a question of this work being particularly of benefit to my own constituency. I trust I can take a broader view than that.
Or any other part of Canada; I said both.

I will go so far as to say that ultimately the construction of a new Welland canal, to give passage to ocean going ships, will be of benefit to this country, but it will not be of any benefit unless you consider the whole system and enter upon the deepening of the entire waterway down to the gulf of St. Lawrence. That cannot be done without the expenditure of six or seven hundred million dollars which the country cannot afford at the present time. If after a few years we see that our financial position is such that we can keep our head above water, then I am prepared to vote for an expenditure of this kind. At present, however, the Government would be well advised to suspend such capital expenditures until we see where we stand financially, and are sure that the money that we do spend in a capital way will be of real benefit to the country.

I am strictly opposed to this vote. I do not think we should consider for a moment voting $5,000,000 for the purpose of construction work on the Welland canal. I would not have spoken on this item but for the fact that I am paired with the member for North Battleford (Mr. Long), and I am not sure whether that arrangement applies to votes taken in the committee. In any event, because of my being so paired, I would not vote on the item; so I want to register my opposition to this expenditure.

So that there may be no misunderstanding, while I am, of course, in favour of my own motion, I want to state that I am paired with an hon. member on the other side and therefore shall not vote.	. ;
Amendment (Mr. Euler) negatived on division.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

No. I want to go on record as being opposed to an expenditure of $5,000,000 on the Welland canal. We have been told that items were passed last year in regard to certain matters and that we did not vote against them. Well, I am certainly opposed to this vote, because I think it is an extravagance on the part of the Government.
Is the hon. member in order after the vote has been taken on the motion?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The question was
upon the amendment to strike the sum of $5,000,000 from the total amount of the resolution. The resolution of which that $5,000,000 is a part is still before the committee, and I must therefore rule the remarks to be in order.
The hon. member seems to be taking a very keen interest in the debates in the last few days, rising to points of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) that the remarks he is now making are certainly not in order. They are not at all relevant to the item under consideration.
' I agree with you, Mr. Chairman, and I also agree with your ruling when you tell the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Currie) that he is out of order and that his point is not well taken.
Order.

Apparently, therefore,
we are both out of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chairman will be obliged to ask the hon. member to discontinue his remarks unless he can bring them to bear upon the resolution under consideration.
I was about, to express compliance with your ruling, Mr. Chairman, when you again rose to call me to order. What I was saying when the hon. member for Simcoe appeared to wake up-
Order.

-was that I was opposed to this vote, and I want to put myself on record to that effect, because if I did not state my views on the subject my position would not appear on the record as having opposed the item. Hon. members on this side of the House have been challenged to vote against different items and I therefore want to let the country know that I am opposed to this particular vote.
Has a contract been let for the construction of the proposed works?

I stated a few moments ago that one contract has been let for one of the sections. The other three tenders have not yet been called for the remaining three sections, but the whole thing will be carried on on the cost plus basis.
What is the amount of the contract let?

The contract is for
$2,442,000, and it will take three years to complete the work.
tUr Currie.l
Has the National Sand and Material Company obtained a contract for any of these works?
Yes they have a small contract for delivering sand.
The minister calls it "a small contract." What would that represent in money?

My officials tell me it is for about 50,000 yards at about seventy cents a yard, which would mean approximately $35,000. That is for sand for sections 1, 2 and 3. There is no contract for sand for the other section-that is entirely a dredging contract. But sections 1, 2 and 3 are for locks and we will require sand and cement for them. Tenders, of course, will be asked for the sand and cement.
I do not know whether the National Sand and Material Company own dredges and operate them at seventy cents a yard.*I would like to know if that is the case?

They have a plant
especially for that work. The sand is taken out of the Niagara river, and a special plant is required for taking that sand from the bottom of the river and placing it in their vessel. Then it has to be taken to shore and delivered to the works.
Can we get the price paid for gravel and the price paid for sand?
We have no contract running at the present time for gravel. The Auditor Generals' Report would show the prices paid last year.

We cannot discuss enquiries that are being carried on at the present time in the Public Accounts Committee. I do not want the minister therefore to mislead the committee by stating that we are discussing the prices that are being paid at the present time-I am not asking for that.
I know but I have not the information here. If I had I would give it to you.

The National Sand and Material Company also appear to be working for the department on the Welland canal improvements. I would like to know why the same company received seventy cents a yard for work done on the Welland ship canal, and in the case of the improvements on the Welland canal supplied 671 cubic yards of gravel at one dollar per cubic yard?

If I remember rightly
it was for this reason: In the one case they had to transship the material to trucks, or something of the kind, and deliver it at the works quite a distance away. There was, therefore, something added to the price for the sand delivered on the dock and for taking it farther on to the works. The gravel was delivered in the canal alongside the works.
Was the extra price paid for sand or for gravel?

The sand is delivered
at the entrance to the canal. The higher price is paid when it is delivered alongside of the work in the canal itself. Extra cost, of course, is involved in transferring it from lake Ontario ports to the works.

According to the explanation given, the National Sand and Material Company was paid seventy cents a cubic yard for sand delivered at a certain place, and in another case one dollar per cubic yard was paid. Now, according to figures appearing at page W-47 of the Auditor General's Report a further sum of $1.50 was paid. It appears that prices vary very often as far as this particular company is concerned. I would like to know why the material is gravel at one time and sand on other occasions?

As I understand there are different places along the works at which material is delivered; it is not all delivered at one particular point. Without having the contract before me I could not speak with any positiveness, but
11 p.m. my officials tell me the difference is because delivery is made at different points along the canal.

Does the minister know
who the directors of this Sand and Material Company are?
I have never heard the name of any member of that firm, nor have I any idea. I do not know whether any of my officials have. Well, the only gentleman they know is Mr. Dick, who seems-
Dick what?

Mr. Dick; that is his
name. He is the man that manages the company; at all events he is the one who seems to deal with the officials of the department.

I see that a total of
$2,642,110.37 has been spent on the contracts awarded, which is a little over the figure mentioned by the minister a short time ago.

What page of the
Auditor General's Report is my hon. friend referring to?
Page W-13.
All right.
The Dominion Dredging Company secured a contract on force account. Were there any tenders called for?

Well, as I have
stated, tenders were originally called for, and the work went on until the war when we settled up with the contractors and closed the work down. After the armistice, when work was resumed, the Canadian Dredging Company, and the others that I named, were put on a cost-plus basis. On January 1, when we renewed their contracts on that basis, it was on the distinct understanding that the time had arrived when we would call for tenders and instructions were given to the engineers to prepare plans and specifications so as to enable that to be done. It takes some little time to do so. One section is ready and the other three sections will be ready in two or three weeks.
That is to say, at a certain time just as the war came on these various contractors were engaged on the work?

Yes.
'Mr. PARENT:	Then, due to the conditions which prevailed during the war, the - department, thinking that these contractors would be losing money, stopped the work and settled up with them. Now the war being over, the department, without asking for tenders, is just letting the same contractors go ahead on a cost-plus basis of eight or ten per cent. Is that the case?

When we closed down the work on account of war conditions it was in order to avoid expending more money at that time. When we started the work again we let it on a cost-plus basis because labour, materials and supplies being so high it would have been impossible to get tenders at anything but a very high figure. Now conditions have changed and we are calling for tenders. These are not the only public works that were closed down at that time.
Yes, but the others were not started again.
Not all of them.

Before the
S.O.S. call was sent out by the minister

to the smoking and voting power of the Government in order to defeat the amendment of my hon. friend from North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), I intended putting a question to the minister, but he was on his feet. The question is, what is the percentage that the contractors are getting on this cost-plus contract?
Eight per cent on a certain part of the work. We supply some of the materials, and of course they do not get any percentage thereon.
Do I understand the minister to state that the Government supplies the cement?
We bought it by tender at the cheapest price and do not pay a percentage on it to the contractors.

According to
the Auditor General's report at page W-47 the Canada Cement Company supplied $14,250.25 worth of cement for the Welland canal. Was that after tenders were called for?
Yes.
What companies tendered and what prices did they quote? I am interested in Canada Cement.
Tenders were received from the Canada Cement Company, the St. Mary's Cement Company, and an other firm-the deputy minister thinks it was Alfred Rogers.
Was the contract given to the lowest tenderer?
Yes, in every case.
Is the minister sure of that?
I am informed so by the deputy minister and the chief engineer, and my recollection is that in all cases where tenders were asked for the lowest tender was accepted.
Does the Government supply a great quantity of these materials besides cement?
Steel ropes, timber and other supplies were taken over at the time the work was closed down. No percentage is paid on those materials.
Was this cement bought through the Purchasing Commission or through the Minister of Marine and Fisheries?

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries had not anything to do with it at all-he never knew we were ordering
fMr. Archambault.]
any cement. The tender accepted was approved by the Purchasing Commission.
The Purchasing Commission had nothing to do with it then?
Yes, they approved it before it was finally settled.

Suppose your
department had sent a requisition to the Purchasing Commission, and afterwards tenders were received and your department approved the lowest tender and sent it to the Purchasing Commission, would the commission refuse to accept that tender the commission refuse to accept that tender?
If they could show any good reason why the lowest tender should not be accepted, the minister or the Government would reconsider it.
What would the minister consider a good reason in such a case?
I would have to depend on the reason given.

Can the minister give
the amount expended on the vote last year , for this work?

Aggregate payments
to contractors to date during the fiscal year of 1920-21, $2,588,588.78. I can give a list of the parties to whom the money was paid if the hon. member wishes.

That may not be necessary for the information I want to put before the committee. I would ask the minister to turn to page W-2 of the Auditor General's report where under Welland Ship Canal Construction he will find that the item represents an expenditure of $3,499,962.35. How can he reconcile this figure with the one he has just given the committee?

I gave the hon. member what was spent between March 31 last year up to the present. The Auditor General's report he is looking at is for the expenditure between April 1, 1919 and March 31, 1920. The Auditor General's report that we would bring down next session would contain the figures I have just given because it would show what was expended on the vote last year.
That would make over $5,000,000.
It would on the two years.

When we ask the minister how much was spent during the fiscal

year, he answers that the total amount expended under the contract was something over $2,000,000, whereas the Auditor General's Report indicates an expenditure of about a million more. The minister says that this is due to their system of accounting. Well, it would almost seem as if they take whatever amount suits their purposes.

Perhaps I did not make myself clear. The Auditor General's Report which was brought down a few days ago shows the expenditures made for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1920, and based on the Estimates presented in 1919. The Auditor General's Report for next year will show the expenditures for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1921, based on Estimates presented in 1920. What I am giving the hon. member, therefore, is what will appear in the Auditor General's -Report next year, based on the items voted last year.

Then the contractors
who have been working on force account have been doing so for quite a long while?
They have been doing work on that basis for two years. From now on, as contracts are let, the work on force account will cease.

When materials are
bought in connection with work done on force account, are the purchases made by the purchasing agent of the department or by the contractors themselves?
Materials other than those we supply are purchased by the contractors, subject to the approval of our engineers in charge of the work.
What percentage would the contractor get on these contracts?
Eight per cent.
How long after the outbreak of war were these contracts cancelled?
In December, 1916, or at the beginning of 1917.
At whose request were the contracts cancelled?
At the request of the Government. Of course, the contractors also wanted them to end.
Why?
The Government did not wish to go on with the expenditure during the war, having regard to war conditions.
Is it not a fact that the principal reason was that the contractors were losing money or feared they would lose money under the contract?

Well, no, I would not say that. When the war was on, men engaged in all these government works enlisted and went overseas, and most of those who remained were required for other war work, munitions and so on. The contractors, of course, did want to shut down, because the tenders were called for prior to the war when conditions were normal and the cost of labour and material following the outbreak of war went up to an abnormal extent.
Was it the policy of the Government generally during the war to cancel contracts of all kinds?
Yes, in the case of work which it was possible to close down on temporarily.
But at the request of contractors who were losing money.

No, I do not want the hon. member to put words in my mouth which I did not say. I do not think he intends to do that. The hon. member will agree that one way of making available the necessary labour for munitions, supplies, and so on during the war was to close down on contracts of this kind.
When was the work reopened?
December, 1918, but they did not commence until January, 1919.
Is it not a fact that in the session of 1918 the sum of $2,000,000 was voted for the Welland canal?
There was a vote in that year, but it was to settle with the contractors for the closing down of the work.

Does the minister remember arguing at that time that he was carrying on this work for the benefit of the returned soldiers? I remember having an argument with the minister on that point when I told him that the returned soldiers did not care to go in for pick and shovel work; that they had had enough of digging ditches. I think the minister's excuse for carrying on this work during the war was in order that returned soldiers might be employed.

So far as*I remember,
it was after the armistice, in the winter of %

1919, that the first vote for resuming work on the Welland canal was put in,

I do not know the minister's department as well as he does; he takes such careful note of everything that goes on in his department that, without having documentary evidence before me, I would not dare to contradict him. The minister stated that during the war the Government did not like to carry on with these public works because of the large expenditures. Did I understand the minister aright?
That was one reason.
And a good one.

The other was just
as good, that we required men for other work in connection with the war.

Does the minister think
that we are in as good a position now financially as we were during the war?

I think so. We are
certainly not spending four or five hundred million dollars per annum on the war.

Does the minister think
that, generally speaking, the financial condition of the country is better now than during the war?

I think we are in
much better shape financially and getting better every day.
What about the railways?

I think the railways
will also improve from time to time.

If the minister argues
that although, during the war, we had no money to carry on with these public works, we have sufficient money for that purpose to-day, I am not at all surprised that he insists on the item passing and that he will not agree to diminish it or to cut it out altogether. Does the department receive monthly reports from the contractors at the present time?

We receive reports
from the engineer in charge of the work.

Did the minister receive
one last month?

We received reports
last month.

From the engineer in
charge of the work on section No. 1?

Mr. Grant, the
engineer in _ charge of the whole work, reports on each contract, and he reported on No. 1.

Has the minister the
figures for No. 1 here?

I have not the report
of last month. I have the report up to March 31.

In the report, was an
item included for the amount of dredging done since the contract was given on a straight contract basis?

The work was on a
cost-plus basis during 1919-20, and we are letting the contractors continue during 1920-21 on a cost-plus basis until we can get the specifications ready to call for tenders. We have been able to call for tenders only for section No. 5. The Canada Dredging Company have been awarded that contract, and it is only now being made out and signed. The contractors are still working on a cost-plus basis.

Nobody is working on
a contract basis at present?

That is so. By next
Wednesday or Thursday, the Canada Dredging company will sign a contract and that part will be on a contract basis.

Do I understand that the
straight contract basis will have a retroactive effect to the first January, 1921?

No. We will call for
tenders on sections Nos. lj 2 and 3 within the next few weeks. The contracts will be let to the lowest tenderer and the cost-plus will cease. If the present contractor does not put in the lowest tender, his contract will end. When the contracts are signed, the work will be on a straight contract basis.

The minister may have
heard this outside or on the street. Is it a fact that there is a great difference between the quantities now being taken out and the quantities taken out when contracts were on a cost-plus basis?

We have not let any
contracts yet on those works, so that I could not compare the quantities. We have no contractors working under anything but a cost-plus basis.

Can the minister give us a comparison of figures between the old contracts, that is the contracts that were let before the war, showing what it was costing us then to carry on this work on a schedule basis, I presume, so much for rock, so much for sand, so much for gravel, and the cost-plus basis? How does the cost-plus compare with the contract that is now let? The country should have

a clear conception of how we are doing this work, what are the schedule prices, what was the original cost before the war, what it was costing us on the cost-plus basis and what are the costs now?

The average price for
tenders that are called now are much higher than they were prior to the war on the old contracts that we cancelled. The present tenders, in fact, are almost double the contract prices prior to the war. One could hardly compare the cost of work done on a cost-plus basis with even the tenders we are receiving now for this reason, that the work had to be started up again and the contracts got ready and in condition to work again. We did not have the same efficiency because we had a serious time to furnish work for men and men were being put on during that time. The cost-plus would be higher than present prices, so that by letting contracts now the work can he done more cheaply than by continuing on the cost-plus basis.

Let us have this a
little more definite if possible. Take section No. 1. The classification of the work was there, sand, gravel, rock and so forth. Under the old contract, what were the schedule prices, the prices for removing a yard of earth, rock or sand or whatever it was? Compare that with the prices for removing the same commodities under the cost-plus basis. I want to know how we were faring in Canada on this work under cost-plus as compared with the contracts.

My officials tell me
that it would not be possible to place the figures side by side, for this reason: When the work was started originally, conditions were not the same as they were when we started on a cost-plus basis. On new work, the hon. member can understand that there is a good deal of material that can be removed very easily, but when you get down quite a piece, the work of removal becomes more costly. I asked my officials to endeavour to give me exactly the information asked for by the hon. menfber, and they told me that it was an absolute impossibility to do that so as to be able to say that a comparison was exact. I wanted to find out whether it was better to continue on a cost-plus basis or to call for tenders. What they tell me is that as nearly as the comparison can be made, the cost-plus last year was much higher than the price we are letting the work for by contract this year. That is as near as I can give it to the hon. member. If it were possible to compare the items side by side, I would be very glad to do it.

When the minister
started this work on force account in the winter of 1919, I remember that I found fault with the commencement of the work then because it was bound to cost too much, and very much more than it would cost under more normal conditions if tenders were called. I want to protest again now.
I venture to say that this work has cost three times as much on force account what it would have cost if proper precautions had been taken and we had waited until a proper opportunity had arrived before calling for tenders. I do not admit that there was such a rush for this work; I believe we could have awaited a more favourable time for calling for tenders. It was not business-like for the department to push this work forward under the circumstances, when they were getting far less work done, and it was costing three times as much as it would have under ordinary and proper conditions.

The minister has just
stated that the contracts now will be very much higher than before the war. That, of course, is to be expected. I would like to ask if the minister is making the change from the cost-plus system to the contract system now because he believes that conditions and prices have become stabilized. Does he believe that costs have been reduced about as far as he expects them to go? Does he not think that the country would be the gainer to the amount of a good many million dollars if he delayed letting contracts until costs came down, when the capital expenditure, of course, would be much reduced and the interest on the investment would be minimized for all the years to come? It not that worth considering?

I consider that prices have become stabilized, and I think that the contractors have come to the same conclusion so that they can make an average for the three years during which the contract is to run. Personally I do not believe that they can come out even on the con. tract, but averaging it up I believe that they think the prices are fair. If we were to carry on with the cost-plus system, it would cost very much more than under this system of contract. The officials tell me, and I have gone into the subject thoroughly that we will save a great deal of money by having the work done by contract instead of on the cost-plus system.

I do not doubt that for a moment. There is no question in the mind of anybody who knows anything about

these things that the cost-plus system would cost a good deal more than the contract system, but does not the minister believe that the present costs will be very much greater than they would be next year, or two or three years from now? If he believes, as I do, that in a few years the work could be done for considerably less than it is being done for now, would it not be worth while considering delaying the work for that period until costs have come down?

We have considered the question from every standpoint. If we were to close down the work, it would cost a very large amount, both to close down and open it up again. There would be a great loss there.
In the deterioration of the work?

Yes, a great loss. That is one thing that made the cost-plus system very much higher. I have had my staff go into the whole question thoroughly, and we have come to the conclusion that this is really the very best thing to do.

May I ask the minister one or two questions in regard to this cost-plus business, or force account? What does the contractor supply in the way of machinery, plant and equipment? Does the contractor supply all that, or does the Government supply some? Who keeps the machinery and plant in repair? On what exactly is the eight per cent figured?
The contractor supplies his own staff. Then, of course, the dredging men have their own plant. We supply a portion of the plant, and they have some of their own.

That is a very general
answer, and only goes to show how absolutely unsatisfactory and how imprudent a method it is, and how the country must view the situation that we have presented to us to-night when you get down to the real details of it. My hon. friend says that the Government supplies some plant, and that the dredging company supplies dredges. I noticed, however, when I was running over hurriedly the year's operations ending March 31, 1920-I have not got all the items, but just a few, because I did not have time-that the commissions paid during that year to the contractor on this cost-plus or force system amounted to $124,624.65.
That includes four contracts.

I have taken all the commissions paid, Und I also find that the Government purchased during the one year for this work, plant and equipment amounting to $274,978.87. There are also large items to engineers, and assistant engineers, that the Government pays out irrespective of the contractors altogether. Then I find one item alone of repairs to machinery amounting to $10,000, but what surprised me most, except that it is a small amount in comparison with the others, is an item for $10,000 for printing and stationery for that one year in connection with the work on the Welland canal. I know how useless it is for a man to go through these items and bring them before the minister for his consideration, but there are the plain bald facts as to this expenditure. I am not in a position to argue whether the Welland canal is a necessity or not. Hon. gentlemen opposite say that it is, while hon. gentlemen on this side who know the situation say that it is not. That is a matter of opinion, a matter for argument. But I do say that the minister should give the committee some sort of a detailed answer. I ask you in all fairness, Mr. Chairman, what kind of answer the minister gave to my question regarding the details of the cost-plus system. What did his answer mean to the country? It could not mean anything to them, and it does not mean anything to us. We do not know who gets this money, who purchases the machinery, or whether it is purchased at the best possible prices. Yet the committee are asked to-night to hand out $5,000,000 to my hon. friend to expend	in the slipshod
manner that the money was expended by him during last year. Now that we are being overtaxed to get sufficient money to meet our liabilities on account of the war, to pay pensions, to pay interest on borowed money-and the Budget which will be brought down on Monday will no doubt impose increased taxation on us-it is unfair to the country for the Government seriously to think of expending $5,000,000 on a work of this nature.
I am not prepared to condemn this proposition, because there may be arguments on either side, and I do not know the location. But I do ask the Government, who are the trustees of the people's money, to consider whether they are not going too rapidly in the direction of large expenditures. It is impossible for one in the short time at his disposal to digest the Auditor General's Report and get all the facts, but it is absolutely unfair and without prece-

dent for a minister, in answer to a question regarding the expenditure of some three and a half million dollars, simply to say that the money was paid out for engineers and staff, and so forth, a vague statement that means nothing to this committee, and absolutely nothing to the country. Parliament is supposed to look into and examine all these expenditures before voting public money and I hazard the statement that there is not a member of the committee who really understands how that money was expended last year, of which the details appear in the Auditor General's Report. When we are asked to vote upwards of $5,000,000, there is hardly a quorum in the House to discuss the question; but if any hon. member suggests that some item be struck out, immediately hon. members on the other side file into the Chamber to oppose the amendment, altogether irrespective of whether it is reasonable or not. Some hon. members may think that this is a proper way of conducting parliamentary business, but it seems to me that it is pretty nearly time the people of the country were aroused to the gravity of the situation in which we find ourselves to-day, and were made aware of the way in which the public business has been carried on during this whole session.

There are some companies which are evidently favourites of the Government. I brought to the attention of the committee a few moments ago an item for the payment of $14,250 to the Canada Cement Company in connection with the Welland canal. I observe on page W.8, another item of $44,279.53, paid to the Canada Cement Company. Was this particular contract awarded to the Canada Cement Company after tenders had been called for?

In connection with all these contracts for cement, tenders were solicited from the different cement companies. The hon. member knows that there are very few cement companies in Canada, and the Canada Cement is the largest. Their tender was the lowest and they got the contract, but there is no favouritism in any respect.
Did the other companies tender?

The Canada Cement
Company and the other companies were all asked to tender. I can assure my hon. friend there is no favouritism at all, either on my part, on the part of the officials, or
on the part of any other member of the Government. The chief engineer and the deputy minister asked for tenders, and, as in every other case, the lowest tenderer got the contract.
How many tenders were there?

the deputy minister
and the chief engineer tell me that there are only three companies they know of that tendered, the Canada Cement, Alfred Rogers, and the St. Mary's Company.

In connection
with this particular contract for $44,000, were there tenders from the other two companies?
Tenders were called for from each of these companies. The officials estimate the total quantities required for the different canals and then call for tenders.
What were the amounts of the other tenders?
I am sorry I have not that information to-night.
It seems to me that the Canada Cement is getting all the cement contracts.

As I understand the hon. member, he wants to know what tenders were submitted and how much per barrel the tender of the Canada Cement Company was, and the same in regard to the St. Mary's and the Rogers companies.
Yes.
I cannot give that information to-night, but if the hon. member will come to the department I will give him the files and let him go through them.
I understand a few other companies tendered?

Yes. I will send a
copy of the tenders to the hon. member.

There is another item on page W.49, of $3,041.81 paid by the Government to the Montreal Warehousing Company for cleaning 304,181 bushels of wheat, and this is charged to construction on the Welland canal. Will the minister explain this item?

On the top of the
same page the hon. member will see that there is reference to the Welland canal, reconstruction to Port Colborne elevator. As a result of an explosion, the whole top of the elevator was blown off. There was

a lot of wheat salvaged and of course it had to be re-cleaned. It was sent down to Montreal to the Warehousing company as they were, I suppose, the only firm that had the machinery to clean this wheat, and as it was part of the damages in connection with the Port Colborne elevator it was charged up to the elevator work. That is the explanation.

I would like to return to
the point raised by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Copp) in connection with the cost-plus system. I think the minister said that eight per cent was paid to the contractors. Does that eight per cent represent a clear profit to the contractors? The minister stated that the contractors themselves supplied certain portions of the plant. Were they paid interest on the amount of their investment over and above the eight per cent they received?

Most of the plant on sections 1, 2 and 3 is plant belonging to the Government which we purchased from them a short time ago. The $124,000 that the hon. member for Westmoreland mentioned as paid to the contractors was divided among the four contractors which would average, say, $31,152 to each. Now the contractors have their own office staff, comprising several employees, and they are paid for their own work in connection with the carrying on of the contract.
They pay for that out of the eight per cent they received?

That is out of the eight per cent, so that the $31,152 which they received on the average, say, if they all got-equal amounts, pays for their own office staff and their own work. The $124,000 does not represent clear profit; in fact only a very small amount would probably be profit. I would consider it a fair wage.

There is one point the
minister did not cover; it is in connection with the plant that is owned by the contractor. I think he said the contractors supplied some portion of the plant. What I asked was this:	What allowance or
remuneration was paid to the contractors for the plant which they supplied over and above the eight per cent?

I erred if I said they supplied plant in addition. They received only eight per cent. We own the plant. When they closed down We bought all

their plant. Sold a portion of it and have since bought some more. We supplied the plant; they did not supply any.

Before the Minister of Justice leaves the chamber I wish to remind the committee that it is now twelve o'clock. We are now entering upon Ascension Day, and I know that my hon. friend would not like to work after twelve o'clock although some hon. members would I would therefore move that the committee rise and report progress.

I was going to suggest to the hon. member that we have been discussing this item all day. I would therefore ask the committee to pass it, and then we have just one more item for the wages of the staff in connection with these canals and repairs. The amount for wages is the same as last year plus the addition involved by reclassification. The item in question is 342; Canals, Staff and repairs -$1,902,500. We have had a fair discussion on the two canals, and if we could pass the two items in question the Minister of Justice then wanted to simply call an item in the Estimates of the Post Office Department so that he could go on with those Estimates. Then I would ask that the committee rise and report progress.
I think that is not an unreasonable request. If the committee agrees to that we could close right now, and we would not be trespassing on Ascension Day, a thing I am very anxious to avoid.
Item 342 looks very simple. It is headed "Staff and Repairs".

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I will have to ask the committee to dispose of item 115 before we discuss any other item.	[DOT]
Regarding item 115 I beg to move that it be reduced by $4,999,999.99.

I could not do very much in the shape of expenditure with a vote of simply one cent. I hope therefore my hon. friend will not press
12 m. his motion. Surely the hon.
gentleman does not propose to allow me only one cent for the Welland canal?

The country
capnot allow even one cent for the Welland canal."

Perhaps the hon.
member will withdraw his motion and allow us to get this item through.
Amendment negatived.
I would like to ask the minister where he is getting the money for this capital expenditure on canal improvements?

When the Finance
Minister is making his Budget speech he will be able to explain that. He arranges all the finances, and these items were all submitted to him before the Estimates were presented to the House.

The Finance Minister is not under any obligation to explain where he is getting the money from, and I do not think it is usual for him to do so. As far as we are concerned we have been trying to squeeze a little money out of Parliament some way or another to relieve the actual distress in the West by getting an extension of railways, but we cannot get the minister to promise us a single dollar. The first excuse given was that we would have to wait until the Railway Estimates came before the House which involved an expenditure of something like $70,000,000. Upon making inquiry recently of the responsible minister-who is possibly as much interested in the particular piece of road in question as anybody in the House-we were informed we would have to. wait until the Supplementary Estimates came down. It seems to be a case of passing the buck, as it were, and having to live on promises. You can get along on hope for a certain length of time, but you will come to the limit eventually. To me it is nothing more or less than a crime to spend $5,000,000 on a work that the country will get absolutely nothing out of. We have been told here repeatedly what an advantage these works are going to be to the West-that we will get our wheat Shipped out so much cheaper if we will just do this, that and the other thing. But, Sir, I find, with all due deference to what the minister told us to-night about the rates coming down, that the rates are going up continuously. There are people in the West who have to spend from thirty to fifty cents a bushel to get their wheat to the railroad simply because the Government declares that it cannot find a dollar to assist them. The Government can find millions of dollars for capital expenditure on canals, but cannot place its hands on a single dollar as far as the West is concerned even when it might relieve western people of that extra expenditure of from thirty to fifty cents a bushel. We have been told here to-night that we will get a reduction of probably a fraction of a cent
on the rates, or something like that, if this expenditure is made. I would like to ask the minister just what benefit this Welland canal is going to be to us? He has told us we will be able to get vessels carrying wheat through to Kingston. I would like to know what sized vessels can unload in Kingston harbour, and what facilities there are at'that port for the handling of grain?

I beg to inform the hon. gentleman that vessels carrying from 75,000 to 100,000 bushels of wheat can go through the Welland canal now. The new Welland canal will permit of the passage of vessels from the upper lakes having a capacity of from 300,000 to 400,000 bushels, and they will be able to go right through to Kingston. At Kingston there are splendid facilities for transferring grain going to Montreal.

Can you unload the largest vessels at the elevators at Kingston?
Hon." Mr. REID : Yes.
You have a larger capacity at Kingston than at any point on Georgian bay?

We have transfer
elevators there and it is not necessary to have very extensive storage as the grain is going by rail. With a cargo of 300,000 bushels on one side of the elevator, as at Port Arthur, and with vessels on the other side receiving it, the grain merely goes through the elevator. At Kingston, I think, there is about 3,000,000 bushels storage.
The minister is not answering my question at all. If you cannot get your boat up to your elevator how are you going to get your grain through the transfer elevator?
There is sufficient depth of water at Kingston.
What is the depth of water at the transfer elevator?
20 to 25 feet.

On the Georgian bay you have just one elevator where you can unload your largest vessel, the Grant Mor-den; if you go to any of the others you have to transfer the grain to smaller boats. However, if Kingston is in that position, so much the better. The minister told us that he remembered the time when we paid twenty cents a bushel to get wheat from Fort William and Port Arthur to Montreal by water. When was that?

About thirty years ago the charge was 20 cents a bushel, and it has been coming down from year to year. The enlargement of the Welland canal brought the rate down to about five or six cents a bushel. That was prior to the war.
The minister states that we can get grain from Fort William to Montreal at five or six cents a bushel?

It has been as low as 31 cents a bushel from Port Arthur and Fort William to Montreal. I know some parties who were interested in a steamer that carried grain probably fifteen years ago between Port Arthur or Fort William and Prescott-where I live, and where grain is also transferred-for two cents a bushel, with a cent and a half from Prescott to Montreal-31 cents a bushel. I have no hesitation in saving that if a person were putting on a vessel at normal prices with wages as they were before the war, five or six cents a bushel would be a good rate.

I have made the statement here myself that it was carried for a fraction of a cent a bushel from Fort William and Port Arthur to the Georgian bay ports. Now the minister is corroborating my statement. But with all the reductions that the minister would like us to believe have been made, we are paying today practically what we paid in 1919 to get our wheat across the lakes. We paid then from Fort William to Georgian bay ports three cents a bushel, last year we paid four and a half cents in September and five and a half cents in October and November. No doubt the agitation that has been going on in this House for control of water rates and for the return of some of the boats that were taken off our own waters has had some effect, but nevertheless there is still a big charge, and we would like the minister to take it into consideration. What department does the merchant marine come under?

It is managed by the
board of directors that manages the Canadian National Railways.
That is, it comes under your department?

While the boats were
under construction and up to the present time they have been under the Minister of Marine, but I understand they will practically all report through the Department of Railways and Canals.

Do I understand the
minister to say that he is going to issue instructions for some of those boats to be brought back to the lakes?
I said I had been consulting with the manager of the merchant marine with a view of bringing them back here if there was any injustice being done in so far as rates were concerned.
If the minister is satisfied there is any injustice in the present rates he is going to bring those boats in, but otherwise not?

That must depend on
those who are managing these vessels. I did say I was drawing the attention of the manager to the rates now charged and asking him to consider the advisability of running some of these vessels in conjunction with the railway system with a view of ensuring that fair and reasonable rates would be charged by water transportation companies between the head of the lakes and Montreal.

Is the committee to
understand that the minister can only suggest that the vessels be brought back?

The vessels are in
exactly the same position as the Canadian National Railway system; I have nothing to do with their operation.
Is this power of suggestion often employed by the minister, and is it a strong or a weak power?

I again wish to call the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that it is Ascension day and that the hon. member on his right (Mr. Morphy) cannot give him absolution for working on this day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am so well satisfied
with the intellectual enjoyment of listening to the many wise observations that are being addressed to the committee that I would not feel called upon to ask for any absolution.

I would suggest to
the Minister of Railways that he accept this item 115 to-night. It is a very large item, and I submit that the minister should accept it and let us go home.
I am always willing to accept any reasonable suggestion. I shall be glad to let all my other items stand if we pass this one. Of course, we wish to call one item in the Post Office Department.
Is it the intention to go on with the Estimates of another department?

We have many departments yet to go into and we are anxious to go on with them. Unless we get into the Estimates of the Post Office to-day there will be no chance to proceed with them until a week from to-morrow. We want to get on; that is the only reason. I am sure hon. members will not think that is unfair.
Does the minister intend that progress shall be reported on his Estimates? Is that the idea?

Yes-pass this item
and then call one item of the Post Office Department Estimates, hut not ask that it be passed; then rise, report progress and go home.
I would ask the Minister of Justice when he expects to go on with the Post Office Department Estimates if he goes into them to-night?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: At the next opportunity that offers.
When will that be?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: On Friday or Saturday, whenever the proper time comes.
Shall we have reasonable notice as to when these Estimates will be taken up?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I give notice now that they will he taken up on Friday, if that is considered reasonable, or, if there is anybody whose convenience would be better suited by saying Saturday, why, I shall try to make any arrangement which will be convenient to everybody.

There is nothing in the annual report of the Post Office Department about the Madrid Conference at which, I understand, very important conclusions were come to, especially with regard to the status of Canada from a postal point of view as compared with that of the other nations. I understand that a resolution was passed under which Canada should not maintain the status she had before. As the matter is of considerable interest, I suggest that my hon. friend get a report of what was done, even if it is only a brief report.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I certainly shall be glad to procure it if possible.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Item number 20- Post Office-
Item No. 115 has not been put to the committee.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I understood that the suggestion of the hon. minister had been unanimously accepted and the item agreed to. The committee could not discuss another item before it was disposed of.
Not at all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We shall return to item 115. Shall the item carry?
Mr.. MAHARG:	When the minister
undertook this work during the session, I think, of 1918, he told us that the object was to give employment to the men who were returning from overseas. Just what proportion of the men employed were returned soldiers?
I may say that every returned soldier who applied for a job on the new Welland ship canal received employment. I got that information from the Soldiers Re-establishment Department.
Returned soldiers with families, 485; civilians with families, 535; single returned soldiers, 343; single civilians, 237.

That is very satisfactory; I have no complaint to make in that respect. There is one other point which I should like to bring up; it is in connection with information which I tried to get when we were discussing the merchant marine. We are spending something like $60,000,000 or $70,000,000 on ships. We are spending millions of dollars every year in connection with our railways, and apparently the matter is entirely out of our hands, since we have appointed a board of directors. Is it possible for the Government to call a halt so far as the management of this merchant marine is concerned?

I really cannot go into the marine end of this Welland canal item; it is not under my department. That information I should say, could have been obtained by my hon. friend from the Minister of Marine when his Estimates were going through. I am sure that he would be glad to give it on some of his other items.

I tried to get the information from the Minister of Marine, but the answer I got was just as evasive as that which the Minister of Railways has

just given. The minister told us to-night that he was going to look into this matter and advise us so-and-so; advice is all that he can give. It seems to me that if the Government have not made up their minds whether they are bosses of the job, it is about time they did. The opinion in our group-and this seems to be the general opinion on this side of the House-is that this is an entirely unwarranted expenditure at this particular time, and we are going to protest against it just as hard as we can. The night is young yet, and we would like to go into this item just a little bit further if possible. Now that tenders are being called for, are any provisions inserted in those tenders as to what class of men shall receive employment when the contracts are being carried out?
No.

The contracts are wide open; the construction may secure men anywhere they like and any class of men that they like. It is reported that in the city of Toronto there are thousands and thousands of ex-service men unemployed. Is no provision being made in these contracts to see that these men secure employment?
There is no such provision. The contractors are requested to carry out the policy that has been laid down, that is, to give returned soldiers work if they apply for it.
Carried.

We will look after the carrying part of the matter after a while. There is plenty of time yet. This evening the hon. member for Algoma East (Mr. Nicholson) took strong exception to the attitude of some of us, and he tried to leave the impression that our attitude was sectional.
