He pointed but that a large number of the items were of a local nature. That is quite true, but there is a corresponding item in one part of the country to offset an item in another part. He illustrated an item of some $35,000 or $40,000 that was being spent for a ferry, and he said: British Columbia has no interest in that. But British Columbia has a big interest in a dry dock that is costing some two or three million dollars, which, I think, will offset that very well, so that we can quite understand why British Columbia is not showing any interest in an expenditure of $35,000 or $40,000. The situation with us on the prairies is quite different. We cannot get even a

branch railroad. They are not being built. We cannot get a dollar for them. Therefore, I think we are quite justified in our_ attitude. As the hon. member (Mr. Davis)' said to-night in connection with the Hudson Bay railway; they are absolutely on a par; in fact, the other was started long before this one, and it is in just as bad a state of repair, but nothing is being done whatever, neither is anything being done as regards the railroads through the prairies. If I understand aright, evidence was given before the Railway Committee the other day that, at the rate grain was being taken out at present, it would take about three years to take this year's grain out of certain parts of the West. If you have millions of dollars to spend on something that is not required at all, surely we can have some little assistance to get out of the country the grain that is there now. For some of this grain you .cannot get one-quarter of the price that would have been received had the grain been , moved out at the proper time. There are men shipping oats now out of Western Canada who are receiving almost nothing for it; in fact, one man was called upon, when the whole transaction was disposed of, to pay $37 or $38 charges to square the account. This was the result of lack of facilities for getting the grain out of the West. Farmers have been drawing grain thirty or forty miles this year when they should not have to draw it more than four or five. There is nothing in this proposition for Western Canada unless the Goveitment spends a couple of hundred million dollars more in deepening the St. Lawrence. There might be something to the proposition then, but it will be many years before the advantage to the West will amount to much. As the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) said, if you can get sufficient business to bring boats to Canada, they will come and not till then.
The hon. member for East Peterborough (Mr. Sexsmith) tried to impress upon us to-night the great advantage that it would be to have our oats ground by the Quaker Oats people. About the only value that we in the West get from the fact that oats are ground is that we get the hulls shipped back to us again in the form of feed and fed to stock under the guise of oat feed, and instead of that assisting them along and helping them to perform their work, it has actually killed stock. About the extent of the value that we get from the grinding of oats is the privilege of having

it ground by a simplex grinder and the hulls sold as other foods when there is absolutely nothing in them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must ask the hon. member to inform the Chairman, how remarks concerning the feeding of stock and the grinding of oats are relevant to the item now before the committee.

If the question had
been asked of the hon. gentleman who introduced the subject, the situation might have been a little different, but it was not. He was permitted to go on and tell us what good this was going to do for us. I am trying to reply by telling him that it would not do us any good. If I am out of order, I will pass on to something else.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think it would be
better if the hon. member did pass on to some other object, because while it is quite true that another hon. member may have said something aside from the question, I fear that is not sufficient justification to allow all other hon. gentlemen to do the same.

Your ruling, Sir, "is
that if one member makes a statement to bolster up his argument, another cannot-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must remind the
hon. member that he is not at liberty to question the ruling. He is at liberty to appeal from it if he so desires.

I am not criticising
your ruling, Sir, at all. I am trying to
understand it, to know where I am so that I will not get in wrong on a future occasion.
I will try something else if that is out of order. The minister in the early part of the evening was telling us what an advantage it would be to us in the West to pass this appropriation. The minister would just give us one illustration, if he can, as to what advantage the Welland canal has been to the West so far-

I really cannot give
any more than I have given several times this evening. I stated that the rate was very high through the original Welland canal. ' Then the canal was enlarged and the rates were materially reduced. I believe, when this work is completed, the rates will be further reduced. That is the only answer that I can give.

Item agreed to.
Civil Government-post office,-salaries, contingencies, including $50 to W. Cooch, $1,435,144.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I presume hon. gentlemen would like to make some comments before the item carries. I do not ask them to discuss the item now. I beg to move the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Progress reported.
